cables.subject: Internal Security Developments in Lebanon
cables.excerpt: Two years before the civil war: Fatah members arrested at Beirut airport with 10 kg of TNT. Black September threatened to blow up the airport. A 2-kg bomb was found and defused. The Lebanese Army G-2 assessed that Arafat may have covertly tipped off Lebanese authorities about a bomb planted by his own movement’s hardliners he could not control.
cables.annotatedBody:
Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State under EO Systematic Review, 30 June 2005 · Now UNCLASSIFIED

Summary
Following several weekend incidents involving fedayeen[1] that produced considerable tension here, Lebanese authorities have instituted heavy security precautions in and around Beirut Airport. The Lebanese Army’s patrolling activities along the Israeli border have also been intensified. We regard these developments as encouraging initial signs on the part of the new Lebanese government.

1.
Beirut International Airport is under strict security on April 30, following a weekend of tension that began the afternoon of April 27 when airport authorities — in the process of conducting a thorough search of departing passengers — arrested three men (2 Lebanese and 1 Palestinian) who were about to board an Air France flight to Paris with 10 kilograms of TNT and detonating devices in their baggage.[2] Upon learning that the individuals were Fatah[3] members, Lebanese Army and security forces — fearing an adverse fedayeen reaction when the arrests became known — moved quickly to block the main access road to the airport and cordon off the southern entrance to the Sabra quarter and the fedayeen stronghold at the nearby Shatila refugee camp.[4]

No reaction occurred that day, but on April 28 airport authorities received a series of anonymous telephone calls threatening that BSO[5] would blow up airport facilities if the arrested fedayeen and their munitions were not released. One such call, made late on April 28, indicated that a bomb had been placed in a water cooler at the airport terminal. A hectic search of the building — supervised personally by Minister of Interior Bashir al-Awar[6] and senior Lebanese security officials — led to the discovery of a 2-kilogram plastic charge timed to explode at 2:30 AM on April 29 in a water cooler.

2.
As of noon on April 30, army and security forces are maintaining intensified security precautions around the entire airport area, with roadblocks established on main access routes, cars being thoroughly searched, and only travelers being allowed to enter the terminal proper. Airline traffic continues as scheduled. The general atmosphere of tension was heightened further on the night of April 28–29 by the explosion of a stick of dynamite thrown at the Jordanian ambassador’s residence from a passing car (no casualties resulted and damage was negligible).

3.
Minister of Interior Awar has stated publicly that the GOL resolved not to give in to blackmail in connection with the April 27 airport incident. We understand from a reliable Presidency source that Awar received orders directly from President Frangieh[7] himself not to yield to the bomb threat.

The Lebanese Army investigation is still in progress, but G-2 believes that the airport bomb was planted by BSO activists acting in defiance of Arafat’s desire to avoid confrontation with the GOL over the April 27 arrests — and that the phone call which led to the bomb’s discovery was possibly an effort by Arafat to assist Lebanese authorities in warding off action by BSO hotheads whose behavior he could not control.[8]

4.
In addition to the GOL’s firmness with the fedayeen over the airport affair, both Lebanese Army and UNTSO[9] sources report that the Lebanese Army has intensified its patrolling in the frontier area over the weekend of April 28–29, with patrols more frequent by night and day.

5. Comment
Although we are unable to say how far the tightening of GOL security precautions will go or how long it will continue — especially if it results in armed clashes between the army and reckless fedayeen elements — we regard it as a heartening initial sign of determination on the part of a new government that has yet to receive a parliamentary vote of confidence.[10]

HOUGHTON[11]

C O N F I D E N T I A L BEIRUT 4974

EO 11652: GDS
TAGS: PINS LE
SUBJECT: INTERNAL SECURITY DEVELOPMENTS IN LEBANON

SUMMARY: FOLLOWING SEVERAL WEEKEND INCIDENTS INVOLVING FEDAYEEN THAT PRODUCED CONSIDERABLE TENSION HERE, LEBANESE AUTHORITIES HAVE INSTITUTED HEAVY SECURITY PRECAUTIONS IN AND AROUND BEIRUT AIRPORT. LEBANESE ARMY'S PATROLLING ACTIVITIES ALONG ISRAELI BORDER HAVE ALSO BEEN INTENSIFIED. WE REGARD THESE DEVELOPMENTS AS ENCOURAGING INITIAL SIGNS ON PART OF NEW LEBANESE GOVT. END SUMMARY.

1. BEIRUT INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT UNDER STRICT SECURITY APR 30 AFTER WEEKEND OF TENSION THAT BEGAN AFTERNOON APR 27, WHEN AIRPORT AUTHORITIES -- IN PROCESS OF CONDUCTING THOROUGH SEARCH OF DEPARTING PASSENGERS -- ARRESTED 3 MEN (2 LEBANESE AND 1 PALESTINIAN) WHO WERE ABOUT TO BOARD AIR FRANCE FLIGHT TO PARIS WITH 10 KGS OF TNT AND DETONATING DEVICES IN THEIR BAGGAGE. UPON LEARNING THAT CULPRITS WERE FATAH MEMBERS, LEBANESE ARMY AND SECURITY FORCES -- FEARING ADVERSE FEDAYEEN REACTION WHEN ARRESTS BECAME KNOWN -- MOVED QUICKLY TO BLOCK MAIN ACCESS ROAD TO AIRPORT AND CORDON OFF SOUTHERN ENTRANCE TO SABRA QUARTER AND FEDAYEEN STRONGHOLD AT NEARBY SHATILA REFUGEE CAMP. NO REACTION OCCURRED THAT DAY, BUT ON APR 28 AIRPORT AUTHORITIES RECEIVED SERIES OF ANONYMOUS TELEPHONE CALLS THREATENING THAT BSO WOULD BLOW UP AIRPORT FACILITIES IF ARRESTED FEDAYEEN AND THEIR MUNITIONS WERE NOT RELEASED. ONE SUCH CALL, MADE LATE APR 28, ACTUALLY INDICATED BOMB HAD BEEN PLACED IN WATER-COOLER AT AIRPORT TERMINAL, AND HECTIC SEARCH OF BUILDING, SUPERVISED PERSONALLY BY MININT BASHIR AL AWAR AND SENIOR LEBANESE SECURITY OFFICIALS, LED TO DISCOVERY OF 2-KG PLASTIC CHARGE TIMED TO EXPLODE AT 0230 HOURS APR 29 IN A WATER COOLER.

2. AS OF NOON APR 30, ARMY AND SECURITY FORCES ARE MAINTAINING INTENSIFIED SECURITY PRECAUTIONS AROUND ENTIRE AIRPORT AREA, WITH ROADBLOCKS ESTABLISHED ON MAIN ACCESS ROUTES, CARS BEING THOROUGHLY SEARCHED, AND ONLY TRAVELLERS BEING ALLOWED TO ENTER TERMINAL PROPER. AIRLINE TRAFFIC CONTINUES AS SCHEDULED. GENERAL ATMOSPHERE OF TENSION, HOWEVER, WAS HEIGHTENED FURTHER NIGHT OF APR 28-29 BY EXPLOSION OF STICK OF DYNAMITE THROWN AT JORDANIAN AMBASSADOR'S RESIDENCE FROM PASSING CAR (NO CASUALTIES RESULTED AND DAMAGE WAS NEGLIGIBLE), AND STRICTER SECURITY MEASURES HAVE BEEN ESTABLISHED IN THAT NEIGHBORHOOD AS WELL.

3. MININT AWAR HAS STATED PUBLICLY THAT GOL HAD RESOLVED NOT TO GIVE IN TO BLACKMAIL IN CONNECTION WITH APR 27 AIRPORT INCIDENT. (WE UNDERSTAND FROM RELIABLE PRESIDENCY SOURCE THAT AWAR RECEIVED ORDERS DIRECTLY FROM PRES FRANGIE HIMSELF NOT TO GIVE IN TO BOMB THREAT.) LEBANESE ARMY INVESTIGATION OF ENTIRE AFFAIR STILL IN PROGRESS, BUT G-2 BELIEVES THAT AIRPORT BOMB WAS PLANTED BY BSO ACTIVISTS ACTING IN DEFIANCE OF ARAFAT'S DESIRE TO AVOID CONFRONTATION WITH GOL OVER APR 27 ARRESTS AND THAT PHONE CALL WHICH LED TO BOMB'S DISCOVERY WAS POSSIBLY EFFORT BY ARAFAT TO ASSIST LEBANESE AUTHORITIES WARD OFF ACTION BY BSO HOT HEADS WHOSE BEHAVIOR HE COULD NOT CONTROL (DETAILS BEING REPORTED VIA SEPARATE CHANNEL).

4. IN ADDITION TO GOL FIRMNESS WITH FEDAYEEN RE AIRPORT AFFAIR, WE HAVE BEEN TOLD BY BOTH LEBANESE ARMY AND UNTSO SOURCES THAT LEBANESE ARMY HAS INTENSIFIED ITS PATROLLING IN FRONTIER AREA OVER WEEKEND APR 28-29. PATROLS MORE FREQUENT BY NIGHT AND DAY.

5. COMMENT: ALTHOUGH WE UNABLE SAY HOW FAR TIGHTENING UP OF GOL SECURITY PRECAUTIONS DESCRIBED ABOVE WILL GO OR HOW LONG IT WILL CONTINUE -- ESPECIALLY IF IT RESULTS IN ARMED CLASHES BETWEEN ARMY AND RECKLESS FEDAYEEN ELEMENTS -- WE REGARD IT AS HEARTENING INITIAL SIGN OF DETERMINATION ON PART OF NEW GOVT THAT HAS YET TO RECEIVE PARLIAMENTARY VOTE OF CONFIDENCE.

HOUGHTON

CONFIDENTIAL NNN
footnotes: Fedayeen (Arabic: فدائيين, “those who sacrifice themselves”): Palestinian armed fighters. In the Lebanese context of 1973, “fedayeen” referred collectively to the armed members of PLO constituent organizations — Fatah, PFLP, DFLP, and others — operating from bases in Lebanese refugee camps under the protection of the 1969 Cairo Agreement.

10 kilograms of TNT with detonating devices constitutes a significant quantity of high explosive capable of catastrophic damage to an aircraft or airport facility. The three individuals — two Lebanese and one Palestinian — were about to board a civilian Air France flight to Paris. This event — a Fatah-linked bomb plot targeting civilian aviation departing from Lebanese soil — is documented in this cable, filed April 30, 1973. It does not appear in the standard historical account of pre-war Lebanon.

Fatah (حركة التحرير الوطني الفلسطيني, Palestinian National Liberation Movement): The largest constituent faction of the PLO, founded in 1959 by Yasser Arafat and others. Fatah was the dominant organization within the PLO and operated the largest armed presence in Lebanon under the Cairo Agreement. The fact that the arrested individuals were identified as Fatah members — not a smaller splinter group — made the incident politically sensitive for Arafat’s leadership of the PLO.

Shatila refugee camp: Palestinian refugee camp established in 1949 on the southwestern outskirts of Beirut. By 1973, Shatila and the adjacent Sabra area had become a significant armed base for Palestinian factions. The Lebanese Army’s immediate cordon of the camp upon the April 27 arrests — anticipating a violent response — documents the Lebanese state’s awareness of the armed capacity in the camps and its own vulnerability to retaliation. The same Shatila camp would be the site of the September 1982 massacre.

BSO: Black September Organization. A covert Fatah-linked terrorist unit established in the aftermath of the 1970–71 Jordanian Army’s expulsion of Palestinian armed groups (“Black September”). The BSO was responsible for the September 1972 Munich Olympics massacre in which 11 Israeli athletes and coaches were killed. By 1973, BSO was active in international terrorism while Arafat maintained official distance from its operations. The BSO’s threat to blow up Beirut International Airport — and its actual planting of a bomb in the airport terminal — is documented in this cable.

Bashir al-Awar: Lebanese Minister of Interior in the cabinet of Prime Minister Amin al-Hafez, formed in April 1973. His personal supervision of the search that discovered the airport bomb documents the seriousness with which the Lebanese government treated the threat. This is the same new government the cable refers to as not yet having received a parliamentary vote of confidence.

President Suleiman Frangieh (1910–1992): President of Lebanon 1970–1976. His direct order to the Interior Minister not to yield to the BSO bomb threat — received from a reliable Presidency source by the Embassy — is documented in this cable. This is the same Frangieh who would be hospitalized during the April 13, 1975 crisis (cable 1975BEIRUT04749) and who would personally handle contacts with Kataeb leader Gemayel during the ceasefire negotiations (cable 1975BEIRUT04860). The 1973 cable establishes his governing pattern: direct engagement and a firm stance toward Palestinian armed pressure — a stance that would become harder to maintain as the 1970s progressed.

This paragraph contains one of the most significant intelligence assessments in the pre-war cable record. The Lebanese Army G-2 believed: (a) the bomb was planted by BSO activists acting against Arafat’s wishes; and (b) the anonymous phone call that led to the bomb’s discovery was possibly Arafat himself covertly assisting Lebanese authorities against his own organization’s hardliners. If the G-2 assessment was accurate, it documents an internal PLO command structure problem in 1973 that is directly continuous with the internal disputes documented in the 1975 cables (cable 1975BEIRUT04860 records an unconfirmed report of a similar Arafat-vs-subordinates dispute during the April 1975 ceasefire negotiations). This assessment is in the diplomatic record as of April 30, 1973. It has not been cited in the standard historical account of PLO operations in Lebanon.

UNTSO: United Nations Truce Supervision Organization. The UN observer mission established in 1948 to monitor the Israel-Arab armistice agreements. UNTSO observers stationed along the Lebanese-Israeli border provided the U.S. Embassy with an independent source for reports on Lebanese Army patrol activity — distinct from Lebanese Army self-reporting.

The cable’s framing of this as the behavior of a “new government” — one that had not yet received a parliamentary vote of confidence — contextualizes the firmness as a deliberate political choice by a government trying to establish its credibility. The Hafez cabinet had been appointed in April 1973 amid a political crisis triggered by Israeli commando raids into Beirut. The government’s willingness to confront the BSO despite its fragile political position is documented here.

Dwight J. Houghton: U.S. Ambassador to Lebanon 1970–1974. Houghton’s posting preceded that of G. McMurtrie Godley (1974–1976), whose cables document the April 1975 crisis. Houghton’s 1973 reporting on PLO behavior and Lebanese government responses provides the pre-war context for understanding the structural conditions that produced the 1975 crisis. His characterization of Lebanese government firmness as “heartening” would prove, in retrospect, to have been reporting on a pattern that the Lebanese state was progressively losing the capacity to sustain.

readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
Two years before the war

On the afternoon of April 27, 1973, airport security at Beirut International Airport found something extraordinary in the baggage of three men about to board an Air France flight to Paris: 10 kilograms of TNT and the devices to detonate it. The men were Fatah members.

What happened over the following 48 hours is documented in this cable, filed by the U.S. Embassy on April 30, 1973. It does not appear in the standard historical account of pre-war Lebanon.

The bomb threat and the bomb that was found

When news of the arrests spread, the Lebanese Army immediately cordoned Shatila refugee camp — a documented acknowledgment that it expected armed retaliation from the camp’s armed organizations. The next day, the Black September Organization called the airport and threatened to blow up its facilities if the arrested men and their explosives were not released.

One call went further: a bomb had been placed in an airport water cooler. The Lebanese Minister of Interior personally supervised the search. They found it: a 2-kilogram plastic charge, timed to explode at 2:30 AM on April 29.

The G-2 assessment: what it means

The Lebanese Army’s military intelligence branch — G-2 — offered a conclusion that is among the most significant in the pre-war diplomatic record. The airport bomb, G-2 assessed, was planted by BSO hardliners acting against Arafat’s explicit wishes. Arafat had been trying to avoid a confrontation with the Lebanese government. And the anonymous phone call that led to the bomb’s discovery was, G-2 believed, possibly Arafat himself — covertly helping Lebanese authorities defuse an action by his own organization’s elements he could not control.

This conclusion — in the Lebanese Army’s intelligence assessment, transmitted through the U.S. Embassy, on record at the State Department as of April 30, 1973 — documents a specific dynamic: Arafat leading an organization with armed factions he could not fully command. Read alongside the 1975 cables, which document a strikingly similar internal PLO command dispute during the April ceasefire negotiations, the pattern spans two years and is consistent.

Frangieh said no

President Suleiman Frangieh gave a direct order to his Interior Minister: do not yield to the blackmail. The Embassy understood this from a reliable Presidency source. The new Lebanese government — which had not yet received a parliamentary vote of confidence — stood firm.

The Embassy called this a “heartening initial sign of determination.” Two years later, during the April 13 crisis, Frangieh would be in the hospital recovering from surgery, the Lebanese Army would have orders to stand aside, and the “determination” the Embassy saw in 1973 would be very difficult to find.

What this cable establishes

The standard historical account of the Lebanese Civil War begins, in most treatments, with April 13, 1975. This cable establishes that the structural conditions of that war — PLO armed factions operating autonomously from Lebanese soil, the Lebanese state attempting to enforce order and being met with armed blackmail, Arafat’s imperfect control over hardline elements within his own movement — were documented realities two full years earlier.

The war did not begin on April 13, 1975. The diplomatic record shows it had been building, documented in real time, since at least 1973.

cables.excerpt: The U.S. Embassy's first-flash report, dispatched at 9:31 PM as fighting erupted across Beirut: martial law declared, rockets fired at the airport, Military Governorate, and vicinity of the Presidency. Most serious fighting in Shatila camp. A Lebanese Army officer named Syria, on the record that night, as 'playing the most unhelpful role.'
cables.annotatedBody:
Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State under EO Systematic Review · Now UNCLASSIFIED

1.
The government announced at 11:30 PM local time a state of emergency (martial law)[1] because “subversive elements tampering with the security of the country.” At approximately 10:00 PM local time, outbreaks of scattered fighting began on the outskirts of the city, with the most serious engagement in the Shatila camp area.[2] A large number of rockets have been fired in and around the city. We have reports that some have been fired at the airport, the Military Governorate of Beirut,[3] and in the general vicinity of the Presidency.[4] The situation seems to be calming down as of midnight, although our information — and that of the GOL — is extremely spotty.[5] We have no reports of any American casualties.

2.
Based on brief talks with the Presidency (Dib[6]) and the Army (Kanaan[7]), the GOL considers the situation “not dangerous but very serious.” They are especially concerned at deliberate, widespread efforts to prevent GOL–fedayeen[8] relations from stabilizing. Kanaan stated that the Syrian government appears to be playing the most unhelpful role in this regard, although he had no time to provide details.[9]

3.
We will report further when we are able to obtain a clearer picture of the situation.[10]

HOUGHTON[11]

footnotes: State of emergency (martial law): The Lebanese government's declaration of a state of emergency transferred effective authority from civilian police and courts to the military. Under this authority, the army could impose curfews, censor the press, and arrest individuals without normal judicial process — all of which are documented in the follow-up cable 1973BEIRUT05159, filed the following morning. The formal justification — "subversive elements tampering with security" — is a government formulation that does not attribute the fighting to a specific party, though the Embassy and Army sources had already identified specific Palestinian factions as the instigators.

Shatila camp: one of the largest Palestinian refugee camps in Beirut, located in the southern suburbs. As the site of the most serious fighting on the night of May 7, Shatila appears here as it would again, nine years later, as the site of the 1982 massacre carried out by Lebanese Forces militiamen while Israeli forces controlled the surrounding area. This cable documents Shatila as an active combat zone in May 1973 — the Lebanese Army engaging Palestinian forces in and around the same camp. This context does not appear in standard accounts of the camp's history.

Military Governorate of Beirut: the headquarters of the military authority governing greater Beirut, a significant institutional target. Rocket fire directed at the Military Governorate — alongside the airport and the vicinity of the Presidency — indicates that the May 7 attacks were not random but targeted the Lebanese state's key security and political nodes.

The Presidency (Baabda Palace) is located in the hills southeast of Beirut. Rocket fire in the general vicinity of the Presidency — the seat of Lebanese executive power — in addition to the airport and military governorate constitutes a direct attack on Lebanese state authority. The cable reports this without attribution at this hour; the follow-up cable (1973BEIRUT05159) identifies the instigating factions as PDFLP, PFLP/GC, and possibly Sa'iqa.

"Our information and that of GOL is extremely spotty": a notable admission of the Embassy's limitations in real-time. Filed at 9:31 PM GMT on May 7 — while the crisis was still unfolding — this cable is the Embassy's immediate dispatch under the NIACT IMMEDIATE protocol, sent before a full picture could be assembled. The subsequent cables (1973BEIRUT05159) were filed when the picture clarified.

Dib: likely a reference to a Lebanese Presidency official or aide who served as an Embassy contact. The name Dib (Arabic: ضيب) appears in the context of the Presidency rather than the army — distinguishing this source from the army contact Kanaan cited in the same sentence.

Kanaan: a Lebanese Army contact who appears in both this cable and the subsequent cable 1973BEIRUT05159. In this cable, Kanaan identifies Syria as "playing the most unhelpful role" in the crisis — one of the earliest explicit on-record attributions of Syrian responsibility that evening. In the follow-up cable filed the next morning, Kanaan confirms that Arafat is trying to calm his troops after the ceasefire.

Fedayeen (Arabic: فدائيين, "those who sacrifice themselves"): Palestinian armed fighters. In the Lebanese context, the term refers collectively to the armed members of PLO constituent organizations operating from bases in Lebanese refugee camps under the framework of the 1969 Cairo Agreement.

"Syrian government appears to be playing the most unhelpful role... although he had no time to provide details": the brevity here is itself a historical fact. Kanaan identified Syria at the moment of the crisis — presumably because the factions involved (PFLP/GC, Sa'iqa) were known to operate with Syrian backing — but the conversation was too brief for elaboration. The fuller picture of Syrian involvement is documented in the subsequent cable (1973BEIRUT05159), where the U.S. Embassy records Syrian Foreign Minister Khaddam's deliberate misrepresentation of negotiating terms and notes Lebanese government suspicion of "a Syrian hand working behind the scene."

The NIACT IMMEDIATE designation required immediate transmission regardless of the hour and regardless of informational completeness. The Embassy sent what it had. readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
9:31 PM, May 7, 1973

The cable was dispatched at the highest urgency level available to American diplomats: Night Action Immediate, requiring attention regardless of the hour. It ran to three paragraphs. The Embassy sent it while the shooting was still audible across the city.

What the Embassy knew at that hour

Fighting had broken out around 10:00 PM local time on the outskirts of Beirut, with the most serious engagement in the area of Shatila refugee camp. A large number of rockets had been fired across the city. Some, the Embassy reported, had been directed at the airport — one of Lebanon's most strategically and economically vital installations. Others had landed near the Military Governorate of Beirut, the headquarters of the army's authority over the capital. Still others had been reported in the general vicinity of the Presidency — the seat of Lebanon's head of state.

The simultaneous targeting of these three nodes — the airport, the military command, the Presidency — was not random. The cable does not say this explicitly, but the pattern it documents implies coordination.

The Army's verdict, that night

In brief contacts with a Presidency aide named Dib and an Army officer named Kanaan, the Embassy obtained one assessment that stands out. Kanaan told the Embassy that the Lebanese government considered the situation "not dangerous but very serious" — and that Lebanese officials were "especially concerned at deliberate, widespread efforts to prevent GOL-fedayeen relations from stabilizing."

Then: the Syrian government, Kanaan said, "appears to be playing the most unhelpful role in this regard." He had no time to elaborate.

This attribution — Syria identified as the most disruptive external actor, on record, at the moment the crisis was unfolding — appears in no standard account of the May 1973 events. It is documented in this cable, filed before midnight on May 7, 1973.

The limits of the moment

The cable is honest about what it does not know. The Embassy's information is "extremely spotty." The government's information, Houghton notes, is also extremely spotty. The cable closes with a direct acknowledgment: "We will report further when we are able to obtain a clearer picture of the situation."

That clearer picture arrived in two cables filed the following morning. Cable 1973BEIRUT05159, dispatched at 8:08 AM on May 8, reported that the Lebanese Army had by then expended aircraft and tank fire against Sabra/Chatila, Bir Hassan, and Borj el Brajne camps. The Prime Minister had resigned at 5:00 AM. A ceasefire came into effect at 8:00 AM. And the Army's G-2 named the specific Palestinian factions responsible for the night's fighting: PDFLP, PFLP/GC, and possibly Sa'iqa — precisely the Syrian-aligned factions Kanaan had pointed toward the night before without being able to say more.

Archival note: This is a State Department cable (from Washington) that relays and forwards to Cairo the text of Beirut cable 5152 — a separate cable sent earlier the same morning of May 7, 1973. The quoted content was drafted by Embassy Beirut (signed HOUGHTON); the outer cable was drafted in Washington by M. Sterner of the Near Eastern and South Asian Affairs bureau and approved by the same officer. The content below is that of the quoted Beirut cable.[1]

Summary
The situation in Lebanon is one of continuing overall calm with occasional incidents, as efforts by Lebanese politicians and Arab “mediators” to “resolve the crisis” continue. Prime Minister Hafez[2] has declared he will not resign, and we understand that President Frangieh[3] remains determined that any modus vivendi[4] concluded with the fedayeen[5] will enable the GOL to place tighter controls on their activity.

2.
As of 0900Z [9:00 AM GMT] on May 7, the situation on the ground remains quiet throughout the country. The only incidents reported on May 6 were:

  • Abduction by Sa’iqa elements[6] of around a dozen Lebanese customs officials from their northern border post at Aboudiyyeh. Syrian authorities freed them shortly afterwards.[7]
  • An early morning explosion and machine-gun attack at the Sidon courthouse (light damage).
  • An exchange of fire between an army patrol and fedayeen approximately 7 kilometers north of the Israeli border in the western sector (at least two fedayeen wounded, according to the army).
  • A brief outbreak of firing from Tal Zaatar camp[8] in the eastern suburbs of Beirut, which drew an army riposte.

All incidents appeared isolated, and no Lebanese casualties were reported. Near midnight on May 6, there was renewed firing in the southeastern Bekaa, but this was quickly brought under control, and Arafat was blaming it on the PFLP/GC and/or PDFLP.[9]

3.
On the political front, collective and individual efforts by Lebanese politicians and Arab “mediators” — including Syrian Foreign Minister Khaddam,[10] Egypt’s Hassan Sabri al-Kholi,[11] and Arab League Secretary General Mahmoud Riad[12] — continue, with numerous meetings on May 5–6 and continuing today.

Prime Minister Hafez made a noteworthy statement on television on the evening of May 5, announcing that he would stay on and expressing hope that problems with the fedayeen could be resolved through mutual cooperation and the help of Arab mediators. He stated his task was to reassure “Palestinian brothers” that President Frangieh, the army, and the Lebanese people support their cause, and to convince the Lebanese that the fedayeen have no intention of infringing on Lebanon’s sovereignty. We noted that in the aftermath of Hafez’s statement, both Rashid Karame[13] and Kamal Jumblatt[14] are no longer pressing him to resign.

4.
We have been told by very reliable sources close to President Frangieh that there will be no new accords or pieces of paper, merely some form of tacit understanding, and that the GOL will — RPT will — succeed in imposing tighter controls on the fedayeen. However, there is no way of predicting at present just what these controls will be in terms of either a new “understanding” or in actual practice.[15]

Both Arab “mediators” and Lebanese politicians appear to have a great deal of talking left in them. At the same time, Frangieh is reliably reported to be taking a firm and clear stand on the basic principle of Lebanese sovereignty, telling all concerned that the GOL has as much right to enforce its sovereignty over Palestinians as such other Arab governments as Syria and Egypt (whose envoys are most active).[16]

The Lebanese Army — upon which Frangieh relies more and more heavily and which will have a major voice in any eventual “understanding” — has not yet been engaged in talks with the fedayeen. Frangieh and the army apparently intend to keep their powder dry until passions have further subsided and politicians and special envoys begin to lose their voice.[17]

HOUGHTON [quoted] / ROGERS[18] [outer cable]

footnotes: This document (1973STATE086221) is a State Department cable from Washington that quotes, verbatim, Embassy Beirut cable 5152 — a cable filed earlier on May 7, 1973, before the fighting that night. The State cable was routed to the U.S. Interests Section in Cairo, which did not receive the original Beirut distribution. The outer cable was drafted and approved by M. Sterner of the Near Eastern Affairs bureau; the quoted content was authored by the Embassy (signed HOUGHTON). The cable ID 1973STATE086221 represents the Washington relay document; the original source is BEIRUT 5152. Both record the same political assessment: the calm that existed on the morning of May 7, before fighting erupted that evening.

Amin al-Hafez (1911–1989): Lebanese Sunni Muslim politician, Prime Minister of Lebanon from April 1973. His television statement on May 5 — announcing he would not resign and framing his role as bridge between the Lebanese state and the Palestinian cause — represented a carefully balanced political position that attempted to maintain both Lebanese Army support and Arab mediator goodwill. Within hours of this cable's source material being written, the fighting of May 7 would make that balance untenable; Hafez resigned at 5:00 AM on May 8 before withdrawing his resignation later that day.

President Suleiman Frangieh (1910–1992): President of Lebanon 1970–1976, a Maronite from northern Lebanon with close ties to the Assad family in Syria. The cable's description of Frangieh's position — seeking tighter controls on Palestinian activity, not new formal agreements — is presented as coming from "very reliable sources close to" him. His private stance of demanding sovereignty enforcement while allowing Arab mediators to manage the public process is documented here in the morning; the night's fighting would force a different public posture.

Modus vivendi (Latin: "way of living"): a diplomatic term for a practical working arrangement between parties who cannot reach a formal agreement, allowing them to coexist without a definitive resolution of underlying disputes. The cable's use of this term — attributed to Frangieh's private position — is precise: Frangieh sought not a treaty but a lived arrangement in which Lebanon could exercise tighter actual control without formal documentation that might constrain him or be cited against him.

Fedayeen (Arabic: فدائيين, "those who sacrifice themselves"): Palestinian armed fighters. In the Lebanese context, the term refers collectively to armed members of PLO constituent organizations operating from bases in Lebanese refugee camps under the framework of the 1969 Cairo Agreement.

Sa'iqa ("Vanguards of the Popular Liberation War"): Syrian Ba'ath-sponsored Palestinian armed faction. The abduction of Lebanese customs officials by Sa'iqa elements from a northern border post — and their release by Syrian authorities — is a textbook example of Syrian dual leverage: Sa'iqa created the provocation, Syrian authorities resolved it, positioning Damascus as both problem and solution. This pattern is documented in the morning's cable as an "isolated incident"; the subsequent night's fighting involved Sa'iqa among other Syrian-aligned factions.

The detail that "Syrian authorities freed them soon afterwards" is diplomatically significant. It establishes a pattern: a Syrian-aligned Palestinian faction acts against Lebanese state personnel and infrastructure; Syrian state authorities then intervene to remedy the incident. This positions Syria as simultaneously enabling the provocation and performing the resolution — a leverage mechanism that the cable records without explicitly characterizing.

Tel Zaatar: Palestinian refugee camp in the Dekwaneh area of northeast Beirut, situated within predominantly Christian-controlled eastern suburbs — one of the geographically most exposed Palestinian camps in the city. Its appearance in a cable of May 1973 firing on Lebanese Army positions is an early instance of the confrontation dynamic that would intensify. In August 1976, Tel Zaatar was besieged and overrun by Maronite militias; approximately 1,500–2,000 Palestinians were killed. This May 1973 cable predates that event by over three years.

Arafat blaming the renewed Bekaa firing on PFLP/GC and/or PDFLP — on the same night that the next cable (1973BEIRUT05155) records the outbreak of full-scale fighting — is a document of Arafat's political positioning in real time. He was deflecting responsibility to the harder-line factions, which the Army's G-2 would confirm the following morning (cable 1973BEIRUT05159) were indeed the primary instigators of the May 7 fighting.

Abdul Halim Khaddam (1932–2020): Syrian Ba'ath politician, Foreign Minister 1970–1984, later Vice President of Syria. His role as an Arab "mediator" in the Lebanese-Palestinian crisis of May 1973 — a role he performed simultaneously with Syrian-aligned Palestinian factions actively attacking Lebanese positions — is documented across this cable series. The next morning's cable (1973BEIRUT05159) records GOL suspicion that Khaddam had publicly announced terms in Damascus far more favorable to the Palestinians than what had actually been agreed, and names the "Syrian hand working behind the scene" as a key Lebanese concern.

Hassan Sabri al-Kholi: Egyptian diplomat and close aide to President Anwar Sadat, serving as Egypt's special envoy in multiple Arab political crises during the early 1970s. His presence as a mediator in Beirut in May 1973 reflects the broader Arab interest in managing Lebanese-Palestinian tensions at a moment when Egypt was preparing for what would become the October 1973 War. The Egyptian role in the 1969 Cairo Agreement — under which Egypt pressured Lebanon to grant the PLO an armed presence on Lebanese soil — gave Cairo a particular stake in the stability of the arrangement it had brokered.

Mahmoud Riad (1917–1992): Egyptian diplomat, Secretary General of the Arab League 1972–1979. His presence as a mediator represents the Arab League's institutional investment in containing the Lebanese-Palestinian confrontation. Like Khaddam and al-Kholi, Riad operated within a framework in which Arab state interests — and not Lebanese sovereignty — were the primary reference point. The cable's use of quotation marks around "mediators" throughout reflects Embassy skepticism about whether the Arab states' role was genuinely aimed at stabilization.

Rashid Karame (1921–1987): Sunni Muslim politician from Tripoli, a former Prime Minister of Lebanon multiple times. A consistent advocate for the Palestinian cause within the Lebanese political system, Karame's decision to stop pressing Hafez to resign — in the aftermath of the PM's May 5 television statement — indicates a temporary stabilization of the Sunni political bloc around Hafez's position. Karame was assassinated in June 1987 by a bomb placed in his helicopter.

Kamal Jumblatt (1917–1977): Druze feudal chieftain of the Chouf, leader of the Progressive Socialist Party, and head of the Lebanese National Movement — the coalition of Lebanese leftist and pan-Arab parties aligned with the PLO. His suspension of pressure on Hafez mirrors the broader temporary stabilization recorded in this cable. On April 13, 1975 — the opening of the civil war — Jumblatt immediately called for the removal of Maronite ministers from the Lebanese cabinet, converting that day's violence into political leverage. He was assassinated in March 1977, almost certainly by Syrian intelligence.

"There will be no new accords or pieces of paper, merely some form of tacit understanding": Frangieh's private position — as relayed to the Embassy by "very reliable sources" — is a direct repudiation of the formal agreement approach embodied by the 1969 Cairo Agreement. He sought practical enforcement over documentary commitments. The irony documented in this cable series is that the crisis ended not with the tacit understanding Frangieh wanted, but with the Melkart Protocol of May 17, 1973 — another "piece of paper" in the tradition of the Cairo Agreement. The fundamental issue of Palestinian armed activity on Lebanese soil remained unresolved.

Frangieh's invocation of Syrian and Egyptian sovereignty enforcement over Palestinians — telling Arab mediators that Lebanon has "as much right" as Syria and Egypt to control Palestinian armed activity — is a pointed rhetorical move. Both Syria and Egypt exercised strict control over Palestinian armed activity within their own territory, refusing to allow the PLO to operate autonomously across their borders or within their populations. The Arab consensus that permitted Palestinian armed activity in Lebanon was therefore explicitly asymmetric: what Lebanon was expected to tolerate was not tolerated by the states most actively pressuring Lebanon to tolerate it.

"Keep their powder dry until passions have further subsided and politicians and special envoys begin to lose their voice": the Embassy's characterization of Frangieh's and the army's strategy — waiting for the diplomatic process to exhaust itself before entering direct talks — proved both accurate and consequential. Within twelve hours of this cable's source being written, the fighting of May 7 had erupted, the army was engaged, and the political framework had collapsed into a military confrontation. The "dry powder" was used sooner than anticipated.

ROGERS: the signature of the outer State Department cable, referring to William P. Rogers (1913–2001), U.S. Secretary of State from January 1969 to September 1973. Cables dispatched from Washington in the Secretary's name were signed ROGERS regardless of whether Rogers personally drafted or reviewed them. M. Sterner (full name: Michael Sterner), who drafted and approved the cable, was a Near Eastern Affairs desk officer.

9:00 AM, May 7, 1973

At nine in the morning, the U.S. Embassy filed a situation report on Lebanon. It recorded calm. The previous day's incidents were isolated. The country was quiet. Arab mediators were in meetings. The Prime Minister had just announced on television that he would not resign. And reliable sources close to the President had told the Embassy something specific about his private position: there would be no new agreements, no documents, merely a practical tighter arrangement.

Twelve hours later, the fighting started.

The calm and its components

The overnight incidents recorded in this cable are individually modest but collectively instructive. Sa'iqa — the Syrian-backed Palestinian faction — abducted a dozen Lebanese customs officials from a northern border post. Syrian authorities freed them. A courthouse in Sidon was attacked. An army patrol exchanged fire with fedayeen near the Israeli border. The Tel Zaatar camp in eastern Beirut briefly fired on army positions.

Each incident was contained. None produced Lebanese casualties. The cable records them as isolated. Viewed in the context of the cables that followed within hours, they are something else: the texture of a situation in which Palestinian factions — including those directly connected to Syrian intelligence — were routinely testing Lebanese state authority, and in which Syrian state actors were simultaneously provoking and resolving incidents to demonstrate leverage.

What Frangieh was saying privately

The cable's fourth paragraph contains a direct report from "very reliable sources close to" President Frangieh. His private position was this: no new accords, no new pieces of paper. A tacit understanding, and tighter practical controls. The Lebanese Army — which Frangieh "relies more and more heavily" upon — was being kept out of the negotiations until the political noise subsided.

It is a strategy of controlled patience. The Army would not enter talks with the fedayeen at this moment of heightened emotion. It would wait. The politicians and special envoys would exhaust themselves. Then the Army would negotiate from a position of restored calm.

By midnight that same day, the Army had declared martial law and was engaged in fighting across the city.

The mediators and their contradictions

The cable names three Arab mediators active in Beirut: Syria's Khaddam, Egypt's al-Kholi, and the Arab League's Mahmoud Riad. It puts "mediators" in quotation marks each time. The Embassy's skepticism is embedded in the punctuation.

Frangieh made the contradiction explicit in private. He told those around him that Lebanon had as much right to enforce its sovereignty over Palestinians as Syria and Egypt did — and that Syria and Egypt, whose envoys were the most active in Beirut pressing Lebanon to accommodate Palestinian armed groups, both exercised strict control over Palestinian military activity within their own borders. The arrangement they were mediating applied to Lebanon what neither was willing to apply to itself.

The document this cable is not

This is a Washington relay cable — a State Department document forwarding Embassy Beirut's morning report to the U.S. Interests Section in Cairo, which lacked direct access to the Beirut cable traffic. The content is Embassy Beirut's (signed HOUGHTON); the outer document is Washington's (signed ROGERS, for Secretary of State William Rogers). It reaches Cairo as the fight is already starting in Beirut.

It was, at the moment of its creation, a record of stability. Within the same calendar day, it became a document of the hours before the Lebanese government declared martial law for the first time in years, and the Lebanese Army began using aircraft and tank fire against Palestinian camps.

Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State under EO Systematic Review · Now UNCLASSIFIED

1.
As of 0700Z [7:00 AM Greenwich Mean Time, May 8], the Beirut area is calm after the Lebanese Army had expended considerable firepower — including aircraft and tank fire[1] — against targets in and around refugee camps in the general southeastern quadrant of Beirut: specifically Sabra/Chatila, Bir Hassan, and Borj el Brajne camps.[2] The rest of the country has thus far remained calm despite the fighting in Beirut, although army units in the South Bekaa are fully alert to possible infiltration from Syria.[3]

2.
At 0500Z [5:00 AM GMT], Prime Minister Hafez resigned,[4] and the cabinet went into session to examine next steps — most important of which could be the designation of a military man as interim Prime Minister.

3.
The fighting which broke out at about 1900Z [7:00 PM GMT] on May 7 appears, in the light of day, to have been a deliberate attempt by some fedayeen elements to torpedo any possibility of stabilizing fedayeen–GOL relations on a new basis.[5] Army G-2 believes that the PDFLP and PFLP/GC[6] were involved, with probably some elements of PFLP and possibly Sa’iqa[7] as well. There are also reports of involvement by armed elements from the LCP.[8]

Between 1900Z and 1930Z, there was widespread firing of rockets and mortars, directed at two or three military installations and the airport but also at random throughout the city. At the same time, several cars full of armed men drove through parts of the city firing at police and other targets. The obvious design was to create panic and touch off a major army–fedayeen confrontation.

4.
At the time the fighting began,[9] Arafat[10] was meeting with several Lebanese political figures — including Saeb Salam[11] and Raymond Edde[12] — to discuss the progress of talks with the GOL on May 7. In these talks — in which Egyptian and Syrian representatives were present — Prime Minister Hafez had reached “some sort of vague first-step agreement” on the route to obtaining a new understanding. According to army participants in the talks, this agreement was nowhere near as detailed or firm — or as pro-fedayeen — as announced by the Syrian Foreign Minister[13] upon his return to Damascus. This is merely one of the reasons for GOL suspicion that a Syrian hand was working behind the scene.[14]

5.
Developments in the immediate future will depend on such factors as: whether Arafat will try and be able to calm the bulk of Fatah fedayeen, keeping as many as possible out of the fighting; whether leftist Lebanese elements (LCP, Ba’ath, PPS, etc.) and Sunni Muslims generally join the fedayeen in continuing the fight with the GOL; and whether the GOL decides actually to move into the camps — which it has not yet done.

Morale of the army continues to be good, with no sign of Muslim/Christian dissension.[15] Reinforcements have been brought into the Beirut area from the south. Army controls around the camps and checkpoints elsewhere are much tighter than before. The atmosphere in Beirut is very tense, with a curfew reimposed and the army — in accordance with the state of emergency — in charge of all security. Emergency law is being used to impose strict censorship on the press and also authorizes the army to arrest virtually anyone suspected of creating trouble. No American casualties reported and no Americans known to be in danger. Embassy well protected. Americans, especially tourists, are quite nervous. We are advising everyone to stay put. Airport closed.

6.
At 0800Z, an EMBOFF talked to the army (Kanaan[16]), who informed us that Arafat is — RPT — is trying to calm his troops. Immediately thereafter, Tony Frangie[17] told us that a new ceasefire came into effect as of 0800Z, and that it is quite possible that the Prime Minister will once again withdraw his resignation.

Tony confirmed that the GOL intends to take a tough line with the fedayeen in any talks and will not give in to demands, reach any sort of formal agreement, or accept the sort of nonsense that Khaddam[18] announced in Damascus has been agreed upon on May 8.[19]

HOUGHTON[20]

footnotes: The cable reads "TAK FIRE" — an apparent teletype transmission error or abbreviation for "TANK FIRE." The corrected reading is supported by context: the cable describes the Lebanese Army employing aviation and armor in combined-arms operations against urban refugee camp targets. Such errors were common in teletype cable transmission of the era and are preserved verbatim in the raw text.

The Lebanese Army's use of aircraft and tank fire against Sabra/Chatila, Bir Hassan, and Borj el Brajne — three Palestinian refugee camps located in the heavily populated southeastern suburbs of Beirut — is one of the most significant facts in this cable. By the morning of May 8, 1973, the Lebanese state had committed its air force and armor against civilian-adjacent camps on Lebanese sovereign territory. This level of military force against Palestinian positions in Beirut had not previously occurred since the Lebanese Army was effectively prohibited from full enforcement by the 1969 Cairo Agreement. The cable reports this as already completed as of 0700Z — the fighting, and the army's response to it, had occurred overnight.

"Army units in South Bekaa fully alert to possible infiltration from Syria": the cable explicitly flags Syria as a potential external source of infiltration in the event of escalation. This concern is elaborated in paragraph 4, where the Embassy records GOL suspicion of a "Syrian hand working behind the scene." The South Bekaa — the Bekaa Valley's southern portion — shares a long border with Syria and was a known route for Palestinian and Syrian-backed armed movements into Lebanon.

Amin al-Hafez (1911–1989): Lebanese Sunni Muslim politician, Prime Minister of Lebanon from April 1973. His cabinet had been attempting to negotiate a revised agreement governing Palestinian armed activity in Lebanon when the May 7 fighting erupted. His resignation at 0500Z on May 8 — in the middle of an active military crisis — represented the collapse of civilian political authority at the moment it was most needed. As paragraph 6 records, he later withdrew the resignation. Al-Hafez should not be confused with Hafez al-Assad, the Syrian President at the time.

The Embassy's assessment that the May 7 fighting was a "deliberate attempt by some fedayeen elements to torpedo any possibility of stabilizing fedayeen-GOL relations" is a significant analytical judgment. It indicates that the Embassy did not regard the outbreak of fighting as accidental, reactive, or attributable to Lebanese Army provocation — but as a purposeful act by specific Palestinian factions intent on preventing a negotiated settlement. This assessment is filed at 0808Z on May 8, within hours of the events described.

PFLP/GC: Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine — General Command. A breakaway faction from the PFLP founded in 1968 by Ahmad Jibril, a former Syrian Army officer. The PFLP/GC split from the PFLP over the latter's ideological emphasis, preferring purely military operations. Operating with close ties to Syrian intelligence and the Syrian military, the PFLP/GC was one of the Palestinian factions most resistant to accommodation with the Lebanese state and most susceptible to direction from Damascus. Its named involvement in the May 7 fighting — alongside the PDFLP and possibly Sa'iqa — is consistent with the cable's concurrent suspicion of Syrian manipulation of events.

Sa'iqa (formally "Vanguards of the Popular Liberation War" — Arabic: طلائع حرب التحرير الشعبية): Syrian Ba'ath Party-sponsored Palestinian armed faction operating in Lebanon. Unlike Fatah, which sought autonomy from Arab state influence, Sa'iqa was effectively an instrument of Syrian policy — its leadership appointed by Damascus and its operations coordinated with Syrian intelligence. Its possible involvement in the May 7 fighting — alongside the PFLP/GC, another Syrian-aligned faction — is one of the facts that generated GOL suspicion of a "Syrian hand working behind the scene," as the cable notes in paragraph 4.

LCP: Lebanese Communist Party (الحزب الشيوعي اللبناني). Founded in 1924, the LCP was a multi-sectarian Marxist party that aligned with the PLO and Palestinian resistance during the 1970s. The cable reports "armed elements" from the LCP as involved in the May 7 fighting — meaning that the confrontation was not exclusively Palestinian, but included Lebanese leftist factions. This is consistent with the pre-civil war pattern in which Palestinian armed organizations and Lebanese leftist parties increasingly coordinated against the Lebanese Army and the Maronite-dominated state.

The cable reads "AT TIME FIRMING BEGAN" — an apparent teletype transmission error for "AT TIME FIGHTING BEGAN." The corrected reading is unambiguous from context: the preceding paragraph describes the outbreak of fighting at 1900Z on May 7, and the subsequent sentence describes Arafat's activities during that fighting. The original error is preserved verbatim in the raw cable text.

Yasser Arafat (1929–2004): Chairman of the Palestine Liberation Organization and leader of Fatah. The cable's description of Arafat meeting with Lebanese political figures — including representatives of both communities — at the precise moment fighting broke out is significant. It places Arafat in a negotiating posture while other Palestinian factions (PDFLP, PFLP/GC, Sa'iqa) initiated military action. Whether Arafat had foreknowledge of the May 7 attacks and was using the negotiations as cover, or was genuinely caught off-guard by factions operating outside his control, is not resolved in this cable — though paragraph 6 reports he was "trying to calm his troops" by 0800Z.

Saeb Salam (1905–2000): Sunni Muslim politician from one of Beirut's most prominent families, a former Prime Minister of Lebanon (1952–1953, 1960–1961, 1970–1973). Salam had recently resigned as Prime Minister in April 1973, just days before the events documented in this cable, specifically over the question of the Lebanese Army's response to Palestinian armed activity — arguing the army was not doing enough. His presence in the negotiations documented in this cable, sitting alongside Arafat when fighting erupted, places a major Lebanese Sunni political figure in direct diplomatic contact with PLO leadership during the crisis.

Raymond Edde (1913–2000): Maronite Christian politician, leader of the National Bloc (Kataeb rival), and a consistently independent voice in Lebanese politics known for his opposition to Syrian influence and his criticism of both PLO armed activity in Lebanon and excessive Maronite intransigence. His presence in the negotiations alongside Arafat and Salam indicates that the talks involved cross-sectarian Lebanese political representation. Edde would later go into voluntary exile in Paris in 1976, citing threats to his life.

The "Syrian Foreign Minister" referred to is Abdul Halim Khaddam (1932–2020), Syrian Ba'ath politician who served as Foreign Minister 1970–1984 before becoming Vice President of Syria. A key operative of the Assad regime's Lebanon policy, Khaddam was closely involved in Syrian manipulation of Lebanese affairs throughout the civil war. The cable's note that Khaddam publicly announced terms in Damascus far more favorable to the fedayeen than what had actually been agreed — and that GOL army participants in the talks confirmed this discrepancy — is a specific documented instance of Syrian disinformation in the context of Lebanese-Palestinian negotiations.

"Syrian hand working behind the scene": the cable records this as GOL's own assessment, not merely Embassy speculation. The simultaneous involvement of PFLP/GC and Sa'iqa — both Syrian-aligned or Syrian-directed factions — in the May 7 fighting, combined with Khaddam's inflation of the agreement terms, constituted a coherent pattern: Syrian interest in preventing a stable Lebanese-Palestinian accommodation that might reduce Syrian leverage over both parties. This cable, filed May 8, 1973, documents U.S. Embassy awareness of Syrian manipulation of Lebanese-Palestinian relations more than two years before the civil war began.

"No sign of Muslim/Christian dissension" within the Lebanese Army: the cable explicitly notes the army's internal cohesion as of May 8, 1973. This cohesion would progressively erode over the following two years as the sectarian polarization of Lebanese society deepened. By early 1976, significant portions of the Lebanese Army — predominantly Muslim officers and enlisted men — mutinied and joined the Palestinian-LNM alliance, fracturing the institution entirely and removing the last restraint on full-scale civil war.

"Kanaan": the Lebanese Army contact referenced here has not been definitively identified. The name may refer to a senior Lebanese Army officer serving in a liaison capacity with the U.S. Embassy. It should not be confused with Ghazi Kanaan (1942–2005), the Syrian intelligence chief who would later dominate Lebanon — though that Syrian officer would not have had this role in 1973.

Tony Frangie (Toni Frangieh, 1942–1978): eldest son of President Suleiman Frangieh, serving at this time as a presidential aide and informal channel between the Lebanese Presidency and the U.S. Embassy. Tony Frangieh was the father of Suleiman Frangieh Jr., the current Lebanese political leader. He was assassinated on June 13, 1978, along with his wife, daughter, and bodyguards, in a pre-dawn raid on his home at Ehden by Bashir Gemayel's Lebanese Forces — one of the most consequential intra-Maronite killings of the civil war, which permanently poisoned relations between the Frangieh and Gemayel clans.

Abdul Halim Khaddam: see footnote 13. The cable's characterization of Khaddam's Damascus announcement as "nonsense" — in the voice of Tony Frangieh relaying the GOL's official position — is a notably blunt diplomatic formulation, preserved verbatim. (The cable reads "NONESENSE" — a teletype spelling error for "NONSENSE," preserved in the raw text.)

The cable's closing note that the GOL "will not give in to demands, reach any sort of formal agreement, or accept" terms as stated by Khaddam reflects a deliberately tough public stance. In fact, the crisis was resolved within days: a ceasefire held, PM Hafez withdrew his resignation, and negotiations produced the Melkart Protocol of May 17, 1973 — an agreement that, like the 1969 Cairo Agreement before it, formally governed Palestinian armed activity on Lebanese soil while falling far short of restoring Lebanese state sovereignty. The pattern documented in this cable — military confrontation followed by negotiated agreement that neither side fully honored — repeated itself until the civil war erupted in April 1975.

The cable is signed HOUGHTON — the same signatory as cable 1973BEIRUT04974 (April 30, 1973). This is likely Roderic L. Houghton, a senior U.S. Foreign Service Officer serving at the Beirut Embassy in 1973. Ambassador William Buffum was the U.S. Ambassador to Lebanon from 1970 to 1974; cables signed by a named official other than the Ambassador typically indicate the Ambassador was absent or that the Deputy Chief of Mission (DCM) or Chargé d'Affaires dispatched the cable. The NIACT IMMEDIATE designation — requiring attention regardless of the hour — confirms the urgency with which the Embassy assessed the situation.

readerNarrative.summary: At 8:08 AM on May 8, 1973, the U.S. Embassy filed this Night Action Immediate cable — the highest available urgency level. By that point, the Lebanese Army had already deployed aircraft and tanks against Palestinian refugee camps in the southeastern suburbs of Beirut: Sabra/Chatila, Bir Hassan, and Borj el Brajne. The Prime Minister had resigned at 5:00 AM. The fighting that produced this had started the previous evening — a deliberate attempt, in the Embassy's assessment, by Palestinian factions including the PDFLP, PFLP/GC, and possibly Syria's client faction Sa'iqa, to torpedo negotiations that were moving toward an accommodation. readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
May 1973: Before the War

The Lebanese Civil War began on April 13, 1975. But the conditions that produced it were visible — and documented — years earlier. This cable, filed at 8:08 in the morning on May 8, 1973, is a window into one of those earlier moments: a night when Palestinian factions opened fire on Lebanese Army positions, the army responded with aircraft and tanks, a prime minister resigned before dawn, and the U.S. Embassy sent a Night Action cable to Washington.

The fighting of May 7, 1973

The fighting began around 7:00 PM on May 7. This cable describes it as a "deliberate attempt" by specific Palestinian factions to torpedo ongoing negotiations between the PLO and the Lebanese government — not a spontaneous escalation, not a response to Lebanese Army provocation. The factions the Embassy's Army sources identified as responsible were the PDFLP and the PFLP/GC, with possible PFLP and Sa'iqa involvement. All were on the harder-line end of the Palestinian spectrum. Two of them — the PFLP/GC and Sa'iqa — operated with close ties to Syrian intelligence.

The method was systematic: rockets and mortars at military installations and the airport, followed by armed vehicles driving through the city firing at police. The stated design, in the cable's words, was "to create panic and touch off a major army-fedayeen confrontation."

The Lebanese Army's response

It succeeded in touching off a confrontation, though perhaps not the one intended. The Lebanese Army responded with aircraft and tanks. By 7:00 AM on May 8, when the Embassy filed this cable, the army had already deployed this firepower against targets in and around three Palestinian refugee camps in Beirut's southeastern suburbs: Sabra/Chatila, Bir Hassan, and Borj el Brajne.

This is a fact that does not appear in the standard account of pre-war Lebanon. The Lebanese Army used aviation and armor against Palestinian camp areas in Beirut in May 1973. The conflict was contained. A ceasefire was arranged. An agreement — the Melkart Protocol — was reached nine days later. And the episode was largely absorbed into Lebanon's managed history of crises that somehow didn't become wars.

Two years later, they did.

Arafat in the negotiations

The cable's paragraph 4 contains a detail that mirrors the pattern documented in the April 30, 1973 cable from this archive: Yasser Arafat was in diplomatic meetings — with Lebanese politicians including Saeb Salam and Raymond Edde, and with Egyptian and Syrian representatives — when the fighting started. As the U.S. Embassy had assessed nine days earlier, hardliners within or adjacent to the Palestinian movement were acting in ways Arafat had not authorized and may have been unable to prevent.

By 8:00 AM on May 8, the Embassy's contact at the Lebanese Army confirmed: Arafat was trying to calm his forces.

The Syrian dimension

The cable documents something that rarely appears in standard historical accounts of May 1973: explicit U.S. Embassy awareness of Syrian manipulation. Paragraph 4 notes that Lebanon's government suspected a "Syrian hand working behind the scene" — and gives specific reasons. The Syrian Foreign Minister, Abdul Halim Khaddam, had publicly announced terms in Damascus far more favorable to the Palestinians than what had actually been agreed in Beirut negotiations. Meanwhile, the factions the Embassy identified as having initiated the fighting — PFLP/GC and Sa'iqa — were precisely those with the closest ties to Damascus.

Syria's interest in preventing a stable Lebanese-Palestinian accommodation was clear: such an accommodation would reduce Syrian leverage over both the PLO and Lebanon. The May 1973 crisis, in this cable's documentation, was not simply a Palestinian-Lebanese confrontation. It was a confrontation in which Syrian-aligned factions were working to prevent the outcome that Arafat and the Lebanese government were moving toward.

The pattern

The crisis ended the way Lebanese crises ended in those years: a ceasefire, a political adjustment, a formal agreement. Prime Minister Hafez withdrew his resignation. The Melkart Protocol of May 17, 1973 was signed — another paper framework governing Palestinian armed activity on Lebanese soil, like the Cairo Agreement before it.

But this cable documents the pattern that the Melkart Protocol did not resolve: Palestinian hardliners willing to use military force to prevent political accommodation; Syrian manipulation of events through proxy factions; a Lebanese state deploying its army against camps and then negotiating as though the army had not just used aircraft and tanks in a residential area of its own capital; a Lebanese political class managing the crisis rather than resolving its causes.

The pattern held for two more years. On April 13, 1975, it stopped holding.

Originally classified SECRET / LIMDIS · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State under EO Systematic Review · Now UNCLASSIFIED · Three sections transmitted as separate cables (BEIRUT 5437 01-03 of 03)

Summary
The situation here is, as we have reported, fluid and confused. Nevertheless, we think an overall assessment of the present and recent past — as best we can make it — will be useful in considering the future implications of the Lebanese crisis. Despite continued calm and progressive return to normalcy, our assessment of the longer-term politico-military situation is not good, although it could improve should certain factors evolve in favor of the GOL.[1]

Reports we receive from the Presidency indicate continued optimism and determination to improve considerably on the balance of power between the GOL and the fedayeen[2] which existed prior to the Beirut raid.[3] However, precise ideas on how to get there are just beginning to emerge, and it may be that the GOL will find it lacks the political and military force required to accomplish this objective.

Internal political situation has been relatively good and confessional split has not occurred, although this is a matter of deep and continuing concern. However, Sunni Muslim leaders are thus far unwilling actually to support Frangieh in imposing control on fedayeen, and Muslim quarters of major cities offer potential refuge as well as some support for fedayeen.

Economic damage and discomfort are generating popular pressure for early settlement on almost any terms so long as calm is restored. Much of the army’s fighting force is tied up in maintaining control over Beirut, although the army has demonstrated its fighting ability, cohesion and courage, and has hurt the fedayeen in some areas. Fedayeen have quieted down and are negotiating with the army. However, they are in a position of relative strength because their combined regular and militia combat elements are more numerous than army combat troops, and are strategically located in big cities as well as in the countryside, while the threat of Syrian action continues to hang heavily over the head of Lebanon.

Arab reaction has been mixed, but even the most helpful Arab states (Egypt and Kuwait) are aiming for a ceasefire along status quo lines rather than a stronger GOL position. There is no visible source of strong external support for Frangieh. The sum of the above factors indicates a likelihood of a compromise solution which will bring only limited improvement in the GOL-fedayeen relationship, but which will leave behind considerable damage to the Lebanese economy, some damage to the strength of the government and morale of the army, and seeds of another explosion later on.[4]

A less likely combination — reduced Syrian threat, rallying of stronger internal and external support for Frangieh’s position, and all-out action by the army — could produce a more favorable long-term outcome.

1. Frangieh’s position and the negotiations
Reports from the Presidency (Dib, Tony Frangie,[5] Foreign Minister Abou Hamad) and the Foreign Office (Saddaqa) indicate that President Frangieh[6] remains determined to enforce GOL control (sovereignty) over the fedayeen to a much greater degree than since 1969. However, precise ideas on the shape of a new overall understanding and how to arrive at one are just beginning to be worked out. We understand Frangieh is insisting upon, at a minimum, quasi-demilitarization of camps in the Beirut area and having fedayeen answer to Lebanese justice for civil offenses. Frangieh is using the National Assembly and consultations with various political and religious leaders in an effort to bolster popular and political support for his position. The Mixed Army-Fedayeen Commission[7] is meeting regularly, but its talks are confined to specifics of maintaining the ceasefire rather than work on an overall settlement.

2. Internal political situation
The internal political situation is somewhat encouraging in that there has been no open split of the Lebanese population along confessional lines,[8] and Sunni Muslim leaders are generally moderate rather than extremist in their attitudes. Former Prime Minister Saeb Salam[9] has been helpful to Frangieh, and former Prime Minister Rachid Karame has been “not as bad as he might have been,” alternating anti-GOL posturing (e.g., urging Hafez to resign as Prime Minister) with efforts to calm Sunni Muslims and prevent an open split. However, none of the Sunni Muslim leaders has come out clearly in support of Frangieh’s position regarding the need to impose greater GOL control on the fedayeen, including the camps.

While Muslim quarters of Beirut, Tripoli, Sidon, and Tyre have generally remained calm, arms were distributed to potentially pro-fedayeen elements in all these cities; and in large parts of Sidon and Tyre, fedayeen and their Sunni and leftist Lebanese supporters have held de facto control with army and police steering clear. The absence of a Sunni Muslim Prime Minister is both indicative of absent Sunni support and one of the reasons for it.

Lack of such support obviously has some inhibiting effect on Frangieh and the army, who fear that pressing the fedayeen too hard could provoke a confessional split and civil strife. It also encourages the fedayeen to hold out for better terms. (We have reliable reports that at one time during the heat of fighting, Arafat threatened Saeb Salam with moving fedayeen in the Beirut area from the camps into the Muslim quarter and making a stand there in individual homes.[10] This is within the capability of the fedayeen, and it is doubtful that Sunnis of Beirut or other cities would offer any resistance, even though only a minority of them could be expected actually to take up arms. The Lebanese Army would, of course, have virtually impossible problems getting the fedayeen out.)

On the other hand, the Christian population is clearly in solid support of the GOL, as one would expect. The Phalange have taken up arms in some sectors and the same is true in some interior regions and villages. Shia Muslim leaders are also supporting the Frangieh position.

3. Economic situation
The economic situation is beginning to bite. Loss of revenue to individuals due to non-work and curfew, plus absence of some foodstuffs and goods due to port closure, is already hurting, as is loss of business and profits to Lebanon’s powerful business community.[11] Given Lebanese mentality, these factors cannot help but generate pressure for an early settlement on almost any terms, so long as calm and commercial activity are restored soon — irrespective of longer-term problems which remain unresolved. A return to business-as-usual can take place without settling the fedayeen problem, but it will make it much more difficult for the army to control fedayeen movement and resupply of camps, and could also make the GOL more apprehensive of risking another showdown with the fedayeen for fear of adverse public reaction.

4. Army performance and limitations
Our overall estimate of the army’s performance to date is good — better even than expected in such fields as air operations, use of armor and infantry in certain tactical operations (such as the attack on the outskirts of Sabra camp on May 8), and use of artillery in the Beirut area and South Bekaa/Arkub.[12] However, the army is not operating on the basis of any operation plan nor any agreed strategic concept for mastering the fedayeen, and it has been held in tight control by President Frangieh, who has thus far not ordered the army to overtake camps by force — probably because he believes the fedayeen will eventually concede minimal demands without such a drastic move, and/or because he fears a direct attack on the camps could provoke a full-scale confrontation throughout the country, a confessional split, and increased Syrian intervention.

A major limitation on the army’s capability is that it has a maximum of 6,000 actual combat troops.[13]

5. Fedayeen strength
The estimate of fedayeen strength in Lebanon we have been using for some time is about 5,000 armed “regulars” plus perhaps another 10,000 “militia” (mostly in the camps).[14] Regardless of the exact numbers, the regulars have increased during the past ten days. The recent fighting has proven correct prior suspicions that the fedayeen (and militia) are heavily armed, including effective anti-tank rockets, Katyusha rockets, heavy and light mortars, and machine guns. Camps are also fortified to varying degrees against assault. During the fighting, fedayeen demonstrated capability for widespread urban guerrilla and terror action even though it was limited in practice. One fedayeen weakness may be a shortage of ammunition after extended fighting.

6. The Syrian role
The Syrian role, as we have all been aware for many years, is of vital importance in determining the relative military strength of the fedayeen and the Lebanese Army.[15] Over the past ten days, apparently without committing more than a couple of hundred Sa’iqa (if that) and few if any regular units, Syria was able to effectively fuel the fighting ability of the fedayeen, harass army installations and outposts near the border area (e.g., two military airfields), and hold over GOL’s head the threat of more massive infiltration of fedayeen and even, should all-out fight develop, Syrian regular units. The Lebanese Army is counting on Israel as a deterrent, but neither the army nor President Frangieh could assume Syrian intervention would not happen, since there were no hard assurances against it from any quarter and there were signals from the Syrians that it might happen. Of vital importance is Syrian smuggling of arms and ammunition. For the present, however, Syria seems content to await developments and display a “visage of sweet reasonableness.”[16]

7. Arab states
Iraq and Algeria were at least as hostile as Syria in terms of propaganda. Egypt and Arab League Secretary General Mahmoud Riad appear to have played a useful role in restraining the Syrians, as did Kuwait. Other Arab states were more or less neutral. However, with the exception of Jordan, none of them have been willing to take a stand backing Frangieh’s demand for tighter controls over the fedayeen; and as fighting continued, the Arab position (including Egypt) vis-à-vis the GOL tended to weaken.[17]

8. Outside powers
The role of outside powers was not a major factor, although France and the United States provided some moral encouragement to Frangieh, while the USSR was discreetly supporting the fedayeen.[18] The USSR’s role could be considered important in that it could have played, and can still play, an effective positive role in supporting Frangieh vis-à-vis the Syrians and fedayeen, but is so far clearly disinclined to do so. For obvious political reasons, the GOL did not ask for direct aid from the U.S. or France, although there were indications it was interested in knowing what we could do to help deter the Syrians.

9. Three scenarios
Some time in the near future — probably a matter of a few weeks, but possibly sooner — the situation summarized above will very likely lead to one of three outcomes:

Option A — Fedayeen acceptance (probably tacit) of Frangieh’s minimal demands: It is our present judgment that the fedayeen will not accept any real demilitarization of camps, even removal of heavy arms, which seems to be the rock-bottom minimum demand of Frangieh. Salah Khalaf[19] told army representatives on the Mixed Commission on May 10 he would never stand for a repetition of what happened to the fedayeen in Jordan in 1970, when they demilitarized camps. The army believes this accurately reflects the real position of the fedayeen. So do we. Therefore Option A seems to us unlikely.

Option B — Frangieh withdrawal (probably tacit) of demands and acceptance of a relationship with the fedayeen fairly close to the status quo ante: This would be difficult for Frangieh, since he is a proud man who has staked a lot on imposing at least minimal GOL sovereignty. Moreover, the army is pressing hard for at least this much compensation for the losses they have suffered, and this much insurance against further Israeli incursions provoked by the fedayeen. Several senior officers and many junior officers are reportedly unhappy over restraints placed on the army over the past ten days. Should Frangieh be forced to back down, it could hurt army morale as well as the President’s prestige. Conditions would exist for another serious explosion at some future date, possibly as a result of another Israeli raid.

Option C — New confrontation between the fedayeen and Frangieh and the army: This is up to Frangieh, whose pride and nationalism could cause him to make a decision even though the odds seemed not to be in his favor. However, we are inclined to doubt he would be willing to take such a risk unless he succeeds in plans to rally stronger political support than he had over the past ten days, and unless he can expect a greater degree of neutralization of the Syrian factor.

10. Conclusion
The principal factors which the President must consider are: (A) avoidance of confessional split, (B) position of Syria (and Egypt) and (C) the capacity of his small army. With these facts in mind, we believe — unless dissident fedayeen elements manage to force a resumption of fighting, which remains a distinct possibility — the most likely outcome is some sort of “Lebanese solution” which will save some face but which is not likely to fundamentally change the position of the fedayeen in Lebanon. It would save Lebanon for the time being from potential catastrophe, but the seeds of another explosion would remain. This, of course, is predicated on the absence of any Israeli raids on Lebanon during the crisis.[20]

HOUGHTON
