BEGIN SUMMARY: SITUATION HERE IS AS WE HAVE REPORTED FLUID AND CONFUSED.
NEVERTHELESS WE THINK OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF PRESENT AND PAST AS BEST WE CAN
MAKE IT, SET OUT, WILL BE USEFUL IN CONSIDERING FUTURE IMPLICATIONS OF LEBANESE
CRISIS. DESPITE CONTINUED CALM AND PROGRESSIVE RETURN TO NORMALCY, OUR
ASSESSMENT OF LONGER-TERM POLITICO-MILITARY SITUATION IS NOT RPT NOT GOOD
ALTHOUGH IT COULD IMPROVE SHOULD CERTAIN FACTORS EVOLVE IN FAVOR OF GOL. REPORTS
WE RECEIVE FROM PRESIDENCY INDICATE CONTINUED OPTIMISM AND DETERMINATION TO
IMPROVE CONSIDERABLY ON BALANCE OF POWER BETWEEN GOL AND FEDAYEEN WHICH EXISTED
PRIOR TO BEIRUT RAID. HOWEVER, PRECISE IDEAS ON HOW TO GET THERE ARE JUST
BEGINNING TO EMERGE AND IT MAY BE THAT GOL WILL FIND IT LACKS POLITICAL AND
MILITARY FORCE REQUIRED TO ACCOMPLISH THIS OBJECTIVE. INTERNAL POLITICAL
SITUATION HAS BEEN RELATIVELY GOOD AND CONFESSIONAL SPLIT HAS NOT OCCURRED
ALTHOUGH THIS IS MATTER OF DEEP AND CONTINUING CONCERN. HOWEVER SUNNI MOSLEM
LEADERS THUS FAR UNWILLING ACTUALLY SUPPORT FRANGIE IN IMPOSING CONTROL ON
FEDAYEEN AND MOSLEM QUARTERS OF MAJOR CITIES OFFER POTENTIAL REFUGE AS WELL AS
SOME SUPPORT FOR FEDAYEEN. ECONOMIC DAMAGE AND DISCOMFORT SUFFERED FOR
CONTINUATION SEEMS TO BE GENERATING POPULAR PRESSURE FOR EARLY SETTLEMENT ON
ALMOST ANY TERMS SO LONG AS CALM RESTORED. MUCH OF ARMY'S FIGHTING FORCE TIED
UP IN MAINTAINING CONTROL OVER BEIRUT, ALTHOUGH ARMY HAS DEMONSTRATED ITS
FIGHTING ABILITY, COHESION AND COURAGE AND HAS HURT FEDAYEEN IN SOME AREAS.
FEDAYEEN HAVE QUIETED DOWN AND ARE NEGOTIATING WITH ARMY. HOWEVER, THEY ARE IN
POSITION OF RELATIVE STRENGTH BECAUSE THEIR COMBINED REGULAR AND MILITIA COMBAT
ELEMENTS ARE MORE NUMEROUS THAN ARMY COMBAT TROOPS AND ARE STRATEGICALLY LOCATED
IN BIG CITIES AS WELL AS IN COUNTRYSIDE, WHILE THREAT OF SYRIAN ACTION CONTINUES
TO HANG HEAVY OVER HEAD OF LEBANESE. ARAB REACTION HAS BEEN MIXED BUT EVEN MOST
HELPFUL ARAB STATES (EGYPT AND KUWAIT) ARE AIMING FOR CEASE-FIRE ALONG LINES
STATUS QUO RATHER THAN STRONGER GOL POSITION. THERE IS NO VISIBLE SOURCE OF
STRONG EXTERNAL SUPPORT FOR FRANGIE. SUM OF ABOVE FACTORS INDICATES LIKELIHOOD
OF COMPROMISE SOLUTION WHICH WILL BRING ONLY LIMITED IMPROVEMENT IN GOL-FEDAYEEN
RELATIONSHIP BUT WHICH WILL LEAVE BEHIND CONSIDERABLE DAMAGE TO LEBANESE
ECONOMY, SOME DAMAGE TO STRENGTH OF GOVERNMENT (I.E., FRANGIE) AND MORALE OF
ARMY, AND SEEDS OF ANOTHER EXPLOSION LATER ON. LESS LIKELY COMBINATION OF
REDUCED SYRIAN THREAT, RALLYING OF STRONGER INTERNAL AND EXTERNAL SUPPORT FOR
FRANGIE'S POSITION, AND ALL-OUT ACTION BY ARMY COULD PRODUCE MORE FAVORABLE
LONG-TERM OUTCOME. END SUMMARY.

1. REPORTS FROM PRESIDENCY (DIB, TONY FRANGIE, FONMIN ABOU HAMAD) AND FOREIGN
OFFICE (SADDAQA) INDICATE THAT PRES FRANGIE REMAINS DETERMINED TO TRY TO
ENFORCE GOL CONTROL (SOVEREIGNTY) OVER FEDAYEEN TO MUCH GREATER DEGREE THAN
SINCE 1969. HOWEVER, IT APPEARS THAT PRECISE IDEAS ON SHAPE OF NEW OVERALL
UNDERSTANDING WITH FEDAYEEN AND HOW TO ARRIVE AT ONE ARE JUST BEGINNING TO BE
WORKED OUT (SEE SEPTEL). WE UNDERSTAND FRANGIE INSISTING UPON MINIMUM OF
QUASI-DEMILITARIZATION OF CAMPS IN BEIRUT AREA AND HAVING FEDAYEEN ANSWER TO
LEBANESE JUSTICE FOR CIVIL OFFENSES. FRANGIE IS USING NATIONAL ASSEMBLY AND
CONSULTATIONS WITH VARIOUS POLITICAL AND RELIGIOUS LEADERS IN EFFORT TO BOLSTER
POPULAR AND POLITICAL SUPPORT FOR HIS POSITION. MIXED ARMY-FEDAYEEN COMMISSION
MEETING REGULARLY BUT ITS TALKS CONFINED TO SPECIFICS OF MAINTAINING CEASE-FIRE
RATHER THAN WORK ON OVERALL SETTLEMENT. ARMY IS AT LEAST AS DETERMINED AS
FRANGIE TO IMPOSE CONTROLS ON FEDAYEEN. HOWEVER IT NOT CLEAR WHAT WILL EMERGE,
ESPECIALLY SINCE GOL-FEDAYEEN NEGOTIATIONS ARE INEVITABLY INFLUENCED BY INTERNAL
POLITICO-ECONOMIC SITUATION AND BY EXTERNAL FACTORS SUCH AS ATTITUDE AND ACTIONS
OF ARAB STATES AND MAJOR POWERS.

2. INTERNAL POLITICAL SITUATION IS, AS WE HAVE REPORTED, SOMEWHAT ENCOURAGING
IN THAT THERE HAS BEEN NO OPEN SPLIT OF LEBANESE POPULATION ALONG CONFESSIONAL
LINES AND SUNNI MOSLEM LEADERS ARE GENERALLY MODERATE RATHER THAN EXTREMIST IN
THEIR ATTITUDES. FORMER PRIME MINISTER SAEB SALAM HAS BEEN HELPFUL TO FRANGIE
AND FORMER PRIME MINISTER RACHID KARAME HAS BEEN NOT AS BAD AS HE MIGHT HAVE
BEEN, ALTERNATING ANTI-GOL POSTURING (E.G., URGING HAFEZ TO RESIGN AS PRIME
MINISTER) WITH EFFORTS TO CALM SUNNI MOSLEMS AND PREVENT OPEN SPLIT. HOWEVER,
NONE OF SUNNI MOSLEM LEADERS HAS COME OUT CLEARLY IN SUPPORT OF FRANGIE'S
POSITION RE NEED TO IMPOSE GREATER GOL CONTROL ON FEDAYEEN, INCLUDING CAMPS.
AND WHILE MOSLEM QUARTERS OF BEIRUT, TRIPOLI, SIDON AND TYRE HAVE GENERALLY
REMAINED CALM, ARMS WERE DISTRIBUTED TO POTENTIALLY PRO-FEDAYEEN ELEMENTS IN
ALL THESE CITIES; AND IN LARGE PARTS OF SIDON AND TYRE FEDAYEEN AND THEIR SUNNI
AND LEFTIST LEBANESE SUPPORTERS HAVE HELD DE FACTO CONTROL WITH ARMY AND POLICE
STEERING CLEAR. ABSENCE OF SUNNI MOSLEM PRIME MINISTER IS BOTH INDICATIVE OF
ABSENCE OF IMPORTANT SUNNI MOSLEM SUPPORT AND ONE OF THE REASONS FOR IT.

(SECTION 2 OF 3)

LACK OF SUCH SUPPORT OBVIOUSLY HAS SOME INHIBITING EFFECT ON PRES FRANGIE AND
ARMY WHO FEAR THAT PRESSING FEDAYEEN TOO HARD COULD PROVOKE CONFESSIONAL SPLIT
AND CIVIL STRIFE. IT ALSO ENCOURAGES FEDAYEEN TO HOLD OUT FOR BETTER TERMS IN
NEGOTIATIONS WITH GOL. (WE HAVE RELIABLE REPORTS THAT AT ONE TIME DURING HEAT
OF FIGHTING ARAFAT THREATENED SAEB SALAM WITH MOVING FEDAYEEN IN BEIRUT AREA
FROM CAMPS INTO MOSLEM QUARTER AND MAKING STAND THERE IN INDIVIDUAL HOMES. THIS
IS WITHIN CAPABILITY OF FEDAYEEN, AND IT IS DOUBTFUL THAT SUNNIS OF BEIRUT OR
OTHER CITIES WOULD OFFER ANY RESISTANCE EVEN THOUGH ONLY MINORITY OF THEM COULD
BE EXPECTED ACTUALLY TO TAKE UP ARMS. LEBANESE ARMY WOULD, OF COURSE, HAVE
VIRTUALLY IMPOSSIBLE PROBLEMS OF GETTING FEDAYEEN OUT.) THERE ARE SOME POLITICAL
FIGURES (AS WELL AS PRESIDENT) WORKING TO RALLY ACTIVE SUNNI MOSLEM SUPPORT FOR
FRANGIE'S POSITION BUT IT HAS NOT YET APPEARED. ON OTHER HAND, CHRISTIAN
POPULATION CLEARLY IN SOLID SUPPORT OF GOL AS ONE WOULD EXPECT. PHALANGE HAVE
TAKEN UP ARMS IN SOME SECTORS AND SAME IN SOME INTERIOR REGIONS AND VILLAGES.
SHIA MOSLEM LEADERS ARE ALSO SUPPORTING FRANGIE POSITION.

3. ECONOMIC SITUATION IS BEGINNING TO BITE. LOSS OF REVENUE TO INDIVIDUALS DUE
TO NON-WORK AND CURFEW PLUS ABSENCE OF SOME FOODSTUFFS AND OTHER GOODS DUE TO
PORT CLOSURE IS ALREADY HURTING, AS IS LOSS OF BUSINESS AND PROFITS TO LEBANON'S
POWERFUL BUSINESS COMMUNITY. LOSS OF REVENUE TO GOL (DIMINISHED TAXES AND
DUTIES) AND TO COUNTRY GENERALLY DUE TO LONGER-TERM FALL-OFF OF BUSINESS AND
TOURISM IS ANOTHER CONSIDERATION, AS IS PERSONAL DISCOMFORT FROM CURFEW AND, IN
SOME CASES, FROM ACTUAL BATTLE DAMAGE. GIVEN LEBANESE MENTALITY, THESE FACTORS
CANNOT HELP BUT GENERATE PRESSURE FOR EARLY SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES BETWEEN
GOL AND FEDAYEEN ON ALMOST ANY TERMS SO LONG AS CALM AND COMMERCIAL ACTIVITY
ARE RESTORED SOON -- IRRESPECTIVE OF LONGER-TERM PROBLEMS WHICH REMAIN
UNRESOLVED. RETURN TO BUSINESS-AS-USUAL CAN TAKE PLACE WITHOUT SETTLING
FEDAYEEN PROBLEM, BUT IT WILL MAKE IT MUCH MORE DIFFICULT FOR ARMY TO CONTROL
MOVEMENT OF FEDAYEEN, RESUPPLY OF CAMPS, ETC., AND COULD ALSO MAKE GOL MORE
APPREHENSIVE OF RISKING ANOTHER SHOWDOWN WITH FEDAYEEN FOR FEAR OF ADVERSE
PUBLIC REACTION.

4. OUR OVERALL ESTIMATE OF ARMY'S PERFORMANCE TO DATE IS GOOD -- BETTER EVEN
THAN EXPECTED IN SUCH FIELDS AS AIR OPERATIONS, USE OF ARMOR AND INFANTRY IN
CERTAIN TACTICAL OPERATIONS SUCH AS ATTACK ON OUTSKIRTS SABRA CAMP MAY 8, AND
USE OF ARTILLERY IN BEIRUT AREA AND SOUTH BEKAA/ARKUB. HOWEVER, ARMY IS NOT
OPERATING ON BASIS OF ANY OPERATION PLAN NOR ANY AGREED STRATEGIC CONCEPT FOR
MASTERING FEDAYEEN, AND IT HAS BEEN HELD IN TIGHT CONTROL BY PRESIDENT FRANGIE
WHO HAS THUS FAR NOT ORDERED ARMY TO TRY AND OVERTAKE CAMPS BY FORCE, PROBABLY
BECAUSE HE BELIEVES FEDAYEEN WILL EVENTUALLY CONCEDE MINIMAL DEMANDS WITHOUT
SUCH DRASTIC MOVE AND/OR BECAUSE HE FEARS THAT DIRECT ATTACK ON CAMPS COULD
PROVOKE FULL-SCALE CONFRONTATION WITH FEDAYEEN THROUGHOUT COUNTRY, CONFESSIONAL
SPLIT, AND INCREASED SYRIAN INTERVENTION. ALSO, AS REPORTED, ARMY SHELLING AND
BOMBING OF CAMP AREAS HAS BEEN HELD TO MINIMUM AND DIRECTED AT SPECIFIC TARGETS
AND AVOIDANCE OF POPULATED AREAS. LIMITED ACTION BY ARMY HAS SUCCEEDED IN
AVOIDING NATION-WIDE CLASH WITH FEDAYEEN AND HAS CONFINED FIGHT WITH FEDAYEEN
IN BEIRUT MOSTLY TO AREAS IN AND IMMEDIATELY AROUND CAMPS RATHER THAN HAVING IT
DEGENERATE INTO FULL-SCALE URBAN GUERILLA ACTION. BEIRUT HAS BEEN BROUGHT UNDER
CONTROL AND FEDAYEEN EFFECTIVELY CONFINED TO CAMPS BUT AT COST OF FREEZING LARGE
PERCENTAGE OF TOTAL ARMY COMBAT UNITS IN BEIRUT AREA AND ALLOWING FEDAYEEN TO
FURTHER FORTIFY CAMPS. THE ARMY HAS BEEN OBLIGED TO BRING ABOUT HALF OF ITS
FORCES IN THE SOUTH INTO BEIRUT, DENUDING THAT SECTION OF COUNTRY TO A POINT
WHERE FEDAYEEN MAY SOON ENJOY GREATER MOBILITY AND FREEDOM OF ACTION (ON THE
LEBANESE SIDE) THAN FOR MANY MONTHS. THE ARMY HAS ALSO BEEN OBLIGED TO "FREEZE"
A NUMBER OF TROOPS IN BORDER AREAS FAR FROM THE MAJOR CITIES IN ORDER TO TRY
AND PREVENT TROOP INFILTRATION FROM SYRIA AND MOVEMENT OF ARMS AND MEN FROM
REMOTE AREAS INTO THE MAJOR CITIES AND REFUGEE CAMPS. ARMY HAS BEEN PARTIALLY
SUCCESSFUL ON BOTH COUNTS BUT ADDITIONAL FEDAYEEN HAVE MOVED FROM SYRIA INTO
REMOTE AREAS OF LEBANON AND SOME ARMS HAVE REACHED THE MAJOR CITIES AND CAMPS.
A MAJOR LIMITATION ON CAPABILITY OF ARMY IS THAT IT HAS MAXIMUM OF 6,000 ACTUAL
COMBAT TROOPS.

5. THE ESTIMATE OF FEDAYEEN STRENGTH IN LEBANON WE HAVE BEEN USING FOR SOME
TIME IS ABOUT 5,000 ARMED "REGULARS" PLUS PERHAPS ANOTHER 10,000 "MILITIA"
(MOSTLY IN THE CAMPS). REGARDLESS OF WHETHER ONE TAKES ISRAEL'S OR LEBANESE
ESTIMATE OF NUMBERS OF FEDAYEEN REGULARS WHO CROSSED INTO LEBANON DURING PAST
TEN DAYS, THE NUMBER OF REGULARS HAS INCREASED. MOREOVER, THERE ARE OTHER
SIZEABLE REGULAR CAMPS IN BEIRUT AREA. RECENT FIGHTING HAS PROVEN CORRECT PRIOR
SUSPICIONS THAT THEY (AND MILITIA) ARE HEAVILY ARMED, INCLUDING EFFECTIVE
ANTI-TANK ROCKETS, KATUSHA, HEAVY AND LIGHT MORTARS AND MACHINE GUNS. CAMPS
ARE ALSO FORTIFIED TO VARYING DEGREES AGAINST ASSAULT. FEDAYEEN (REGULARS AND
MILITIA) HAVE ALSO PROVEN THEY ARE ABLE TO HOLD THEIR GROUND UNDER FIRE
(ALTHOUGH NOT DIRECT ASSAULT) IN CAMPS. ALTHOUGH SOME OF CAMPS (AND FEDAYEEN
IN THEM) SUFFERED CONSIDERABLE DAMAGE. DURING FIGHTING FEDAYEEN DEMONSTRATED
CAPABILITY FOR WIDESPREAD URBAN GUERILLA AND TERROR ACTION EVEN THOUGH IT WAS
LIMITED IN PRACTICE. SAME APPLIES FOR EFFECTIVE ACTION IN OTHER MAJOR CITIES
(E.G., SIDON AND TYRE) AND IN COUNTRYSIDE (E.G., AMBUSH BETWEEN SIDON AND TYRE)
ALTHOUGH THERE WERE ONLY LIMITED INSTANCES OF FEDAYEEN ATTACKS OUTSIDE BEIRUT
EXCEPT FOR ACTION IN SYRIAN BORDER AREAS. ONE FEDAYEEN WEAKNESS MAY BE SHORTAGE
OF AMMUNITION AFTER EXTENDED FIGHTING.

(SECTION 3 OF 3)

6. SYRIAN ROLE, AS WE HAVE ALL BEEN AWARE FOR MANY YEARS, IS OF VITAL IMPORTANCE
IN DETERMINING RELATIVE MILITARY STRENGTH OF FEDAYEEN AND LEBANESE ARMY. OVER
PAST TEN DAYS, APPARENTLY WITHOUT COMMITTING MORE THAN A COUPLE OF HUNDRED SAIQA
(IF THAT) AND FEW IF ANY REGULAR UNITS, SYRIA WAS ABLE TO EFFECTIVELY FUEL
FIGHTING ABILITY OF FEDAYEEN, HARASS ARMY INSTALLATIONS AND OUTPOSTS NEAR BORDER
AREA (E.G., TWO MILITARY AIRFIELDS), AND HOLD OVER GOL HEAD THREAT OF MORE
MASSIVE INFILTRATION OF FEDAYEEN AND EVEN, SHOULD ALL-OUT FIGHT DEVELOP, SYRIAN
REGULAR UNITS. THIS LATTER PROSPECT DISCOUNTED SOMEWHAT BY LEBANESE ARMY WHO
COUNTING ON ISRAEL BUT NEITHER ARMY NOR PRESIDENT FRANGIE COULD ASSUME IT WOULD
NOT HAPPEN SINCE THERE WERE NO HARD ASSURANCES AGAINST IT FROM ANY QUARTER AND
THERE WERE SIGNALS FROM SYRIANS THAT IT MIGHT HAPPEN. MAIN POINT TO BEAR IN
MIND, HOWEVER, IS THAT EVEN WITHOUT COMMITTING REGULARS SYRIA HAS SHOWN
CAPABILITY OF ADDING CONSIDERABLY TO MILITARY CAPABILITY OF FEDAYEEN. SYRIA ALSO
HAS CAPABILITY OF ADDING TO POLITICAL THREAT POSED BY PRO-FEDAYEEN AND/OR
LEFTIST LEBANESE ELEMENTS BY ITS PROPAGANDA AND ITS POLITICAL AGITATION AMONG
MAJOR CITIES. OF VITAL IMPORTANCE IS SYRIAN SMUGGLING OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION.
JUDGING FROM WHAT WE KNOW HERE AND WHAT IDF HAS REPORTED VIA DAO TEL AVIV,
SYRIANS SEEM TO HAVE PLENTY OF FEDAYEEN UNITS IN RESERVE SHOULD FIGHTING START
UP AGAIN. FOR PRESENT, HOWEVER, THEY SEEM CONTENT TO AWAIT DEVELOPMENTS AND
DISPLAY VISAGE OF SWEET REASONABLENESS.

7. ROLE OF OTHER ARAB STATES HAS, AS REPORTED FROM HERE AND OTHER POSTS, VARIED
WIDELY. IRAQ AND ALGERIA WERE AT LEAST AS NASTY AS SYRIA IN TERMS OF PROPAGANDA,
ALTHOUGH ALGERIANS WERE LESS PROVOCATIVE IN TERMS OF AMBASSADOR YAZID'S
BEHAVIOUR ON THE GROUND. EGYPT AND MAHMOUD RIAD SO FAR APPEAR TO HAVE PLAYED
USEFUL ROLE IN RESTRAINING SYRIANS AS DID KUWAIT. OTHER ARAB STATES WERE MORE
OR LESS NEUTRAL. HOWEVER, WITH EXCEPTION OF JORDAN, NONE OF THEM, AS BEST WE
CAN DETERMINE, HAVE BEEN WILLING TO TAKE STAND IN EITHER PUBLIC OR PRIVATE
BACKING FRANGIE'S DEMAND FOR TIGHTER CONTROLS OVER FEDAYEEN AND, AS FIGHTING
CONTINUED, ARAB POSITION (INCLUDING EGYPT) VIS-A-VIS GOL TENDED TO WEAKEN.

8. ROLE OF OUTSIDE POWERS WAS NOT A MAJOR FACTOR ALTHOUGH FRANCE AND UNITED
STATES PROVIDED SOME MORAL ENCOURAGEMENT TO FRANGIE WHILE USSR WAS DISCREETLY
SUPPORTING FEDAYEEN. ROLE OF LATTER COULD BE CONSIDERED IMPORTANT IN THAT IT
COULD HAVE PLAYED AND CAN STILL PLAY EFFECTIVE POSITIVE ROLE IN SUPPORTING
FRANGIE VIS-A-VIS SYRIANS AND FEDAYEEN BUT SO FAR CLEARLY DISINCLINED TO DO SO.
FOR OBVIOUS POLITICAL REASONS GOL DID NOT ASK FOR DIRECT AID FROM US OR FRENCH
ALTHOUGH THERE WERE INDICATIONS THAT IT WAS INTERESTED IN KNOWING WHAT WE COULD
DO TO HELP DETER SYRIANS.

9. SOME TIME IN NEAR FUTURE, PROBABLY MATTER OF FEW WEEKS BUT POSSIBLY SOONER,
SITUATION SUMMARIZED ABOVE WILL VERY LIKELY LEAD TO: (A) FEDAYEEN ACCEPTANCE
(PROBABLY TACIT) OF FRANGIE'S MINIMAL DEMANDS; OR (B) FRANGIE WITHDRAWAL
(PROBABLY TACIT) OF DEMANDS AND ACCEPTANCE OF RELATIONSHIP WITH FEDAYEEN FAIRLY
CLOSE TO STATUS QUO ANTE; OR (C) NEW CONFRONTATION BETWEEN FEDAYEEN AND FRANGIE
AND ARMY.

A. OPTION A) IT IS OUR PRESENT JUDGMENT THAT FEDAYEEN WILL NOT RPT NOT ACCEPT
ANY REAL DEMILITARIZATION OF CAMPS, EVEN REMOVAL OF HEAVY ARMS WHICH SEEMS BE
ROCK-BOTTOM MINIMUM DEMAND OF FRANGIE. (SALAH KHALAF TOLD ARMY REPS ON MIXED
COMMISSION ON MAY 10 HE WOULD NEVER STAND FOR REPETITION OF WHAT HAPPENED TO
FEDAYEEN IN JORDAN IN 1970 WHEN THEY DEMILITARIZED CAMPS. ARMY BELIEVES THIS
ACCURATELY REFLECTS REAL POSITION OF FEDAYEEN. SO DO WE.) THEREFORE OPTION A)
ABOVE SEEMS TO US UNLIKELY.

B. OPTION B) THIS WOULD BE DIFFICULT FOR FRANGIE SINCE HE IS PROUD MAN WHO HAS
STAKED A LOT ON IMPOSING AT LEAST MINIMAL GOL SOVEREIGNTY OVER FEDAYEEN,
INCLUDING CAMPS. MOREOVER, ARMY IS PRESSING HARD FOR AT LEAST THIS MUCH
COMPENSATION FOR LOSSES THEY HAVE SUFFERED -- AND THIS MUCH INSURANCE AGAINST
FURTHER ISRAELI INCURSIONS PROVOKED BY FEDAYEEN. SEVERAL SENIOR OFFICERS AND
MANY JUNIOR OFFICERS REPORTEDLY UNHAPPY OVER RESTRAINTS PLACED ON ARMY OVER
PAST TEN DAYS. SHOULD FRANGIE BE FORCED BACK DOWN IT COULD HURT MORALE OF ARMY
AS WELL AS PRESTIGE OF PRESIDENT. ECONOMIC LOSSES WOULD BE FOR NAUGHT. MOREOVER
CONDITIONS WOULD EXIST FOR ANOTHER SERIOUS EXPLOSION AT SOME FUTURE DATE BETWEEN
GOL AND FEDAYEEN, POSSIBLY AS RESULT OF ANOTHER ISRAELI RAID.

C. OPTION C) THIS IS UP TO FRANGIE WHOSE PRIDE AND NATIONALISM COULD CAUSE HIM
TO MAKE DECISION EVEN THOUGH ODDS SEEMED NOT TO BE IN HIS FAVOR. HOWEVER, WE
ARE INCLINED TO DOUBT HE WOULD BE WILLING TO TAKE SUCH RISK UNLESS HE SUCCEEDS
IN PLANS TO RALLY STRONGER POLITICAL SUPPORT THAN HE HAD OVER PAST TEN DAYS,
AND UNLESS HE CAN EXPECT GREATER DEGREE OF NEUTRALIZATION OF SYRIAN FACTOR THAN
WAS CASE OVER PAST TEN DAYS.

10. IN CONCLUSION, PRINCIPAL FACTORS WHICH PRESIDENT MUST CONSIDER IN CHARTING
COURSE OF ACTION ARE (A) AVOIDANCE OF CONFESSIONAL SPLIT, (B) POSITION OF SYRIA
(AND EGYPT) AND (C) CAPACITY OF HIS SMALL ARMY. WITH THESE FACTS IN MIND, WE
BELIEVE, UNLESS DISSIDENT FEDAYEEN ELEMENTS MANAGE TO FORCE RESUMPTION OF
FIGHTING -- AND THIS IS A DISTINCT POSSIBILITY -- MOST LIKELY OUTCOME IS SOME
SORT OF "LEBANESE SOLUTION" WHICH WILL SAVE SOME FACE BUT WHICH IS NOT LIKELY
TO FUNDAMENTALLY CHANGE POSITION OF FEDAYEEN IN LEBANON. IT WOULD SAVE LEBANON
FOR THE TIME BEING FROM POTENTIAL CATASTROPHE BUT SEEDS OF ANOTHER EXPLOSION
WOULD REMAIN. THIS, OF COURSE, PREDICATED ON ABSENCE OF ANY ISRAELI RAIDS ON
LEBANON DURING CRISIS.

HOUGHTON

NOTE BY OC/T: NOT PASSED CAIRO.

footnotes: This cable is classified SECRET with a LIMDIS (Limited Distribution) handling restriction — the first SECRET-classified cable in this archive. The LIMDIS restriction limits distribution beyond the standard addressee list; the cable was explicitly not passed to Cairo (noted at the end of each section). This more restricted distribution reflects the analytical sensitivity of what follows: a frank, comprehensive assessment of Lebanon's likely political trajectory.

Fedayeen (Arabic: فدائيين, "those who sacrifice themselves"): Palestinian armed fighters. In the Lebanese context of May 1973, the term refers collectively to the armed members of PLO constituent organizations operating from bases in Lebanese refugee camps under the framework of the 1969 Cairo Agreement. By May 1973, their combined regular and militia forces in Lebanon significantly outnumbered the Lebanese Army's available combat troops, as this cable documents.

"The Beirut raid": a reference to the April 9–10, 1973 Israeli commando operation in Beirut (Operation Spring of Youth), in which elite IDF units landed by sea and assassinated three senior PLO leaders in their Beirut apartments: Muhammad Yusuf al-Najjar (Abu Yusuf), Kamal Adwan, and Kamal Nasser. The operation demonstrated the Lebanese state's inability to protect either its own sovereignty or the Palestinian leadership operating on Lebanese soil — and was a proximate cause of the Palestinian armed escalation documented in the May 1973 crisis cables.

"Seeds of another explosion later on": filed May 12, 1973. The next major Lebanese-Palestinian confrontation occurred in April 1975. This prediction, embedded in the cable's summary, is one of the most consequential sentences in this archive.

Tony Frangie (Toni Frangieh, 1942–1978): eldest son of President Suleiman Frangieh, serving as a presidential aide and an informal Embassy contact. He appears in multiple cables in this archive serving as a conduit between the Lebanese Presidency and U.S. diplomats. He was assassinated on June 13, 1978, along with his wife, daughter, and bodyguards, in a raid on his home at Ehden ordered by Bashir Gemayel — one of the most consequential acts of intra-Maronite violence of the civil war.

President Suleiman Frangieh (1910–1992): President of Lebanon 1970–1976, a Maronite from the Zgharta region of northern Lebanon. The cable's frank assessment — "he is a proud man who has staked a lot" — captures the personal dimension of the political crisis: Frangieh had committed his presidency to imposing sovereignty over the fedayeen, and a climb-down would be personally as well as politically costly. The cable documents both his determination and the structural constraints preventing him from achieving his stated objective.

Mixed Army-Fedayeen Commission: the joint body established during the May 1973 crisis for negotiations between the Lebanese Army and PLO constituent organizations. The cable notes the Commission is confined to maintaining the ceasefire rather than addressing the underlying relationship — a diplomatic holding pattern that the subsequent cables (1973BEIRUT05755-05776) document yielding the fedayeen "unilateral promises" of May 17, 1973, which became the Melkart Protocol.

The "confessional split" concern runs through the entire May 1973 cable series as the central constraint on Lebanese state action. The Lebanese political system was built on a carefully managed balance of Maronite, Sunni, and Shia interests (the 1943 National Pact); any military action by the Lebanese Army against Palestinian fighters risked being perceived as a Maronite attack on Muslim and Arab solidarity, fracturing the internal political consensus. This fear effectively capped the army's freedom of action and gave the fedayeen structural protection beyond their own military capability.

Saeb Salam (1905–2000): Sunni Muslim politician from one of Beirut's most prominent families, former Prime Minister multiple times. The cable's description — Salam "has been helpful to Frangieh" despite being a former PM who had resigned the premiership specifically over the Lebanese Army's response to Palestinian armed activity — illustrates the complexity of Sunni political positioning: supporting the state in private while unable to support it publicly on the Palestinian issue.

"Arafat threatened Saeb Salam with moving fedayeen from camps into the Muslim quarter": this threat — documented here as a reliable Embassy report — is one of the most analytically significant facts in this cable. It establishes that Arafat explicitly used the prospect of fedayeen dispersal into civilian Muslim neighborhoods as diplomatic leverage against Lebanese Sunni political leaders. If fedayeen were dispersed through Beirut's Muslim quarters, the Lebanese Army could not engage them without devastating those neighborhoods and producing the confessional split that both Frangieh and Lebanon's Sunni leaders were working to avoid. Arafat's threat was therefore militarily credible and politically unanswerable.

The Lebanese economy in 1973 was heavily dependent on tourism, banking, and transit trade — all of which were acutely sensitive to political instability and security disruption. The cable's observation that economic pressure would generate demand for a settlement "on almost any terms" proved accurate: the Melkart Protocol of May 17, 1973, was reached partly because the Lebanese business community and public were unwilling to absorb the costs of continued confrontation. The cable explicitly notes this dynamic as one that would compromise long-term security outcomes.

"Attack on the outskirts of Sabra camp, May 8": a specific operation cited as an example of the army's tactical competence. This attack occurred the same night that cable 1973BEIRUT05159 reported the Lebanese Army had deployed aircraft and tanks against the camps — meaning the May 8 ground action against Sabra was part of the same military operation sequence. This cable, filed May 12, is offering a retrospective assessment of those operations.

"Maximum of 6,000 actual combat troops": this figure — embedded in a SECRET cable — represents the U.S. Embassy's assessment of Lebanon's effective military capacity in May 1973. Against an estimated 15,000 fedayeen (5,000 regulars plus 10,000 militia), the arithmetic was stark. The Embassy's assessment that the army lacked the capacity to overtake all fedayeen-held camps by force was not a political judgment — it was a quantitative one.

"5,000 armed regulars plus perhaps another 10,000 militia": the Embassy's fedayeen strength estimate in May 1973 — 15,000 total armed combatants — exceeds the Lebanese Army's 6,000 combat troops by 2.5 to 1. This numerical imbalance is the military foundation of the cable's assessment that the fedayeen were in "a position of relative strength." It is also the foundational fact underlying Lebanon's inability to enforce the Cairo Agreement, the Melkart Protocol, or any subsequent agreement: the party being asked to comply had more guns than the party doing the asking.

"As we have all been aware for many years": the phrasing — addressing other U.S. government agencies in a SECRET cable — signals that what follows is not new intelligence but a consolidated frank assessment of something already known within the national security community. The Syrian role in multiplying Lebanese fedayeen military capacity, documented here in quantitative terms, was systemic and sustained.

"Display a visage of sweet reasonableness": the Embassy's sardonic characterization of Syria's post-crisis posture — having fueled the fedayeen fighting ability and threatened direct military intervention, Damascus now presented itself as a constructive regional actor. This pattern — Syrian destabilization followed by Syrian "mediation" — would recur throughout the Lebanese crisis. Khaddam's performance in the pre-fight diplomatic exchanges (documented in cables 1973STATE086221 and 1973BEIRUT05159) exemplifies exactly this dynamic.

"The Arab position (including Egypt) vis-à-vis the GOL tended to weaken as fighting continued": this is a candid assessment of the limits of Egyptian moderation. Egypt had played a "useful role in restraining Syrians" earlier in the crisis (per the May 7 cable), but as fighting continued, Arab solidarity with the Palestinian cause reasserted itself. The U.S. Embassy is documenting in May 1973 the structural constraint that would remain constant through 1975: Lebanon was fighting for its sovereignty against forces that Arab solidarity, however ambivalent, could not ultimately be mobilized to oppose.

"USSR was discreetly supporting the fedayeen": the embedding of Soviet support within a SECRET assessment — "discreetly," "not a major factor," but capable of playing "an effective positive role" that it was "clearly disinclined" to play — documents the Embassy's understanding of Soviet interests in Lebanon. The USSR had leverage over Damascus, over leftist Lebanese parties (the Lebanese Communist Party is specifically cited), and over fedayeen factions. Its choice to apply that leverage in support of fedayeen positions rather than Lebanese state authority was a policy choice, documented here.

Salah Khalaf (1933–1991), known by his nom de guerre Abu Iyad: one of the founding members of Fatah and a close associate of Arafat, Khalaf served as the PLO's intelligence chief and was the principal organizer of Black September Organization operations including the 1972 Munich Olympics massacre. His statement to the Lebanese Army Mixed Commission on May 10, 1973 — that he "would never stand for a repetition of what happened to the fedayeen in Jordan in 1970 when they demilitarized camps" — is one of the most important facts in this cable. It refers to the events of Black September 1970, when the Jordanian Army's suppression of the PLO resulted in thousands of Palestinian casualties and the PLO's forced expulsion from Jordan. Khalaf's warning was not rhetorical; it was a statement of organizational survival doctrine. The Embassy took it seriously: "So do we."

The cable's closing conditional — "predicated on the absence of any Israeli raids on Lebanon during the crisis" — would prove exactly relevant to the next explosion. On April 11, 1974, Israeli forces attacked the town of Kiryat Shmona in a Palestinian raid, prompting Israeli reprisals. More directly, on April 11, 1974, the DFLP attacked the northern Israeli town of Kiryat Shmonah. Israeli reprisals in Lebanon were constant triggers for Lebanese-fedayeen tensions. This cable, written in May 1973, explicitly anticipates this mechanism. The civil war that began on April 13, 1975, was in no small part the product of exactly the dynamic this cable lays out: a face-saving Lebanese solution, seeds of another explosion, and the underlying structural conditions unchanged.

readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
May 12, 1973: Five Days After

Five days after the Lebanese Army had deployed aircraft and tanks against Palestinian camps in Beirut, the U.S. Embassy filed this assessment. Not a situation report. Not a cable about a specific meeting or event. A comprehensive verdict on what had happened, what it meant, and what would come next.

It was classified SECRET with a Limited Distribution handling restriction. It ran to three sections transmitted as separate cables. It was explicitly not passed to Cairo. And it closed with a sentence that proved, twenty-three months later, to be exactly correct.

The arithmetic that constrained everything

Beneath the political analysis, the cable rests on two numbers. The Lebanese Army had a maximum of 6,000 actual combat troops. The fedayeen had an estimated 15,000 — 5,000 regulars and 10,000 militia, mostly in the camps. Against a ratio of 2.5 to 1, armed with anti-tank rockets, Katyusha rockets, and fortified camps, the fedayeen could not be dislodged by force without a military commitment Lebanon did not have and without political consequences Lebanon could not absorb.

The Embassy knew this. Frangieh knew this. The army knew this. And the fedayeen knew it too. The May 10 statement by Salah Khalaf — Abu Iyad, the PLO's intelligence chief — to the Mixed Commission made the fedayeen position explicit: he would "never stand for a repetition of what happened to the fedayeen in Jordan in 1970 when they demilitarized camps." The Embassy's gloss on this was two words: "So do we." Real demilitarization was therefore assessed as unlikely.

The threat that paralyzed Sunni politics

The cable contains a detail about Arafat and Saeb Salam that is not in the standard account of May 1973. During the fighting, the Embassy received reliable reports that Arafat threatened Salam — a former Prime Minister and one of Lebanon's most prominent Sunni figures — with moving the fedayeen from the camps into Beirut's Muslim neighborhoods and making a stand there, house by house.

The threat was militarily credible and politically unanswerable. The Lebanese Army could not engage fedayeen dispersed through Beirut's Muslim residential areas without devastating those neighborhoods. And while only a minority of the Sunni population would be expected to actively take up arms alongside the fedayeen, the Embassy judged the population would not resist their presence — meaning the army would have "virtually impossible problems getting the fedayeen out." Arafat had found the precise leverage point that paralyzed Lebanese state action: the threat of a confessional split so severe that it was more dangerous than the alternative.

The three scenarios

The cable lays out three possible outcomes with unusual analytical precision for diplomatic reporting, and then rates each. Option A — real demilitarization of camps — is judged unlikely, for the reasons above. Option B — Frangieh backing down to something close to the status quo — is described as hard for a proud man who has staked his presidency on the outcome, but is implicitly the most politically available path. Option C — a new confrontation — depends on factors Frangieh doesn't currently have: stronger political support, a neutralized Syrian threat.

The assessment's conclusion is that Option B is where events are heading — not because it's good, but because it's what the constraints allow. And it would leave "conditions for another serious explosion at some future date."

Syria's structural role

The cable's sixth paragraph is one of the most precise assessments of Syrian leverage in pre-war Lebanon in the documentary record. Without committing more than a few hundred Sa'iqa fighters — possibly fewer — and without deploying regular army units, Syria had been able to multiply the fedayeen's fighting effectiveness, harass Lebanese military airfields, and hold the threat of massive intervention over Lebanon's head. The Lebanese Army was counting on Israel as a deterrent against Syrian regular intervention; but neither Frangieh nor the army could assume that deterrent would hold, because there were "signals from the Syrians that it might happen" and "no hard assurances against it from any quarter."

Syria's then-posture — "content to await developments and display a visage of sweet reasonableness" — is the Embassy's description of the aftermath: having applied maximum pressure during the crisis, Damascus was now performing moderation. The cable documents this performance without the illusion that it represented a change of intent.

The verdict

The cable's final paragraph is worth quoting in full:

"Most likely outcome is some sort of 'Lebanese solution' which will save some face but which is not likely to fundamentally change the position of the fedayeen in Lebanon. It would save Lebanon for the time being from potential catastrophe but seeds of another explosion would remain."

Filed May 12, 1973. The Lebanese Civil War began April 13, 1975. The Melkart Protocol — the agreement reached six days after this cable — changed nothing structurally, as the companion cables (1973BEIRUT05755-05776) document in real time. The "seeds" the Embassy identified in May 1973 grew for twenty-three months before they produced the explosion.

This cable is the record of someone who saw it coming and wrote it down.

Archival Note — Merged Entry

This is a merged archival entry combining two companion cables filed 90 minutes apart on May 18, 1973. Cable 1973BEIRUT05755 (181315Z) documents the diplomatic conversation: what the GOL had achieved and what U.S. support was being requested. Cable 1973BEIRUT05776 (181500Z) documents the substance: the specific fedayeen commitments that formed the basis of the Melkart Protocol. The two cables are explicitly cross-referenced as SEPTEL companions in the original texts. They are presented together here because neither is fully intelligible without the other.

Cable 1 of 2 — 1973BEIRUT05755 — 181315Z May 73

Subject: GOL Request for USG Assistance — Ref: State 94202

Summary
The GOL has obtained from Fatah, PFLP, and PDFLP specific concessions (SEPTEL)[1] which go beyond the minimal demands reported earlier. It is on the basis of the fedayeen acceptance of these specific points that the GOL would like us to make the demarches[2] discussed in the reference cable. The demarches would be in support of full implementation of promises made by the fedayeen organizations, which the GOL intends to provide to Arab and certain other governments through its own diplomatic channels. The USSR is still considered the top priority, since the GOL considers it to have the greatest potential influence on the actions of the fedayeen and of Syria. This is all the more important since Sa’iqa[3] has not explicitly accepted the promises made by the others, and the SARG position remains very unclear. Concerning Israel, the Chargé[4] informed Fonmin and Dib of our estimate of the Israeli position regarding Lebanon and indicated we had recently been in touch with the Israelis on the general problem.

1.
The Chargé and Embassy officer met the morning of May 18 with Foreign Minister Abou Hamad,[5] Presidency Director-General Dib,[6] and Foreign Office Secretary-General Sadaqa to inform them of the substance of the reference cable. The Chargé also said that since the last meeting on May 15 we had approached the USSR again in Moscow and had been in contact with the Israelis regarding the general problem the GOL is currently facing. The Chargé gave the group the Department’s estimate of Israeli intentions along the lines of paragraph 6 of the reference cable. Sadaqa asked what the USG would do should the situation change — for example, if there were Syrian intervention and Israel felt obliged to take military action in Lebanon. The Chargé replied that our basic position remains one of supporting Lebanese political independence and territorial integrity, but that it is not possible to say what action we would take in the vague hypothetical circumstances Sadaqa had mentioned. The Foreign Minister appeared well satisfied with our position vis-à-vis Israel.

2.
After informing the GOL of our willingness to make the requested demarches, the Chargé asked the Foreign Minister if he could be clearer about the sort of demarche the GOL had in mind and when they should be made, particularly in view of reports that the GOL and the fedayeen had reached agreement in the Mixed Commission[7] the evening of May 17. The Foreign Minister asked Dib to explain just where the GOL stood with the fedayeen, since this was essential background for determining how to pitch the demarche. Dib’s report is being sent SEPTEL, but in summary the GOL has obtained from the fedayeen greater concessions than those listed as minimal demands. The fedayeen concessions are in the form of unilateral promises to undertake certain actions, and not in the form of a new GOL-fedayeen agreement.[8] The Army is to prepare a paper incorporating these promises, which the GOL will provide to Arab governments and certain other governments so that there will be no misunderstanding as to the substance of the future relationship between the GOL and the fedayeen. However, now that the fedayeen have accepted, the most important problem begins: bringing about implementation of the promises and assuring there is no backsliding. The Army and fedayeen are working on modalities and a timetable for implementation at the present time. Another outstanding problem is the fact that Sa’iqa and PFLP/GC have not directly and explicitly agreed to the commitments made by the others. Fatah, PFLP, and PDFLP representatives on the Mixed Commission state they are speaking for all fedayeen organizations, but the GOL does not accept this as necessarily so. The problem of PFLP/GC is of lesser magnitude than that of Sa’iqa, since the latter reflects the attitude of the Syrian government and of course has more men.

3.
Abou Hamad said he thought USG demarches to Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Abu Dhabi, and Iran (and any further talks we might have with Jordan) should stress the vital importance to Lebanon and the entire region of the implementation of the fedayeen promises — since GOL failure to establish its sovereignty over its own territory and those living therein (as other Arab governments have done) would surely result in the ultimate destruction of the pro-Western, democratic, free-enterprise principles on which the Lebanese system rests, and would create a new source of major tension in the area which none of the countries to be approached would want. The GOL has no intention of “liquidating” the fedayeen movement and wishes to preserve good relations with them within the limitations dictated by Lebanese sovereignty. The GOL has already spoken to Arab governments explaining its case, and will do so again early next week while passing along a copy of the fedayeen promises. A subsequent supporting demarche by the USG — and if possible by other governments (we assume he meant France and England and perhaps other Western Europeans) — would add considerable weight. The important thing is to ensure that the fedayeen keep their promises in fact and that as time goes on they are not allowed to backslide. The GOL intends to supervise this very closely but will need support from governments that contribute most to fedayeen coffers.

4.
Concerning the Soviets, Abou Hamad said they continue to be the most important government in terms of their ability to influence the situation for good or ill. They had direct influence on the fedayeen in Lebanon as well as on their left-wing allies such as the Lebanese Communist Party and Kamal Jumblatt.[9] They also have major indirect influence through their strong position in Damascus and Baghdad, which are the major sources of external trouble for Lebanon. One of President Frangieh’s specific objectives is to obtain an explicit commitment by Sa’iqa to the promises made by other fedayeen organizations — and this would depend upon the attitude of the SARG. The USSR could be very helpful on this specific point as well as in counselling moderation generally on the SARG and others.

5.
Abou Hamad and Dib closed the meeting by thanking us for all the support the USG has already provided and for whatever more we can do. They reported their conviction that the only way to avoid another, more serious explosion in Lebanon is for the fedayeen to actually make good on their promises and then try not to back away from them with the passage of time.[10] Support from the various outside governments to be approached by the USG will be vital in this process.

HOUGHTON

Cable 2 of 2 — 1973BEIRUT05776 — 181500Z May 73

Subject: GOL-Fedayeen Arrangement — Ref: State 94202

Summary
Fedayeen representatives in the Mixed Commission came up with a list of specific promises on the evening of May 17 on actions they would take in accordance with President Frangieh’s demand that GOL sovereignty henceforth be fully respected. The list covers: a commitment not to undertake cross-border raids; to stay well back from sensitive border areas; to cease using Beirut as an information/propaganda headquarters; to remove heavy weapons from camps; to acknowledge the supremacy of Lebanese law over Palestinians; to remove all “foreign elements” (i.e., non-Arabs); and to allow Lebanese security forces access to camps. The GOL is fully aware that the fedayeen promises must be implemented and then be respected over time to be worthwhile, and that fedayeen good faith in this regard is suspect.[11] The Army is presently working out a detailed agreement whereby the fedayeen will be supposed to implement their promises. These commitments by the fedayeen apply to all 15 refugee camps, not only those in the Beirut area.

1.
In the conversation with the Foreign Minister reported SEPTEL, Director General of the Presidency Dib briefed the Chargé and Embassy officer the morning of May 18 on the status of the GOL-fedayeen talks that concluded the evening of May 17. Dib and the Foreign Minister both stressed on several occasions that there was no agreement or even understanding between the GOL and the fedayeen. Rather, the latter had made a series of commitments or promises to Army negotiators, which the GOL has accepted as the basis for a new relationship between itself and all fedayeen in Lebanon. The commitments made on the evening of May 17 will be drawn up on paper by the Army, and we and certain other governments will receive copies. The Army is talking right now to fedayeen representatives about the modalities of implementation, including a timetable. Dib then summed up (from memory) the essential points of the fedayeen commitments. (These are reported as follows but may not be complete nor completely accurate. We shall obtain further information and precision when available.)

2. Activity in Camps
The fedayeen have agreed to cease all training in the camps, to remove “heavy weapons” from the camps, and to cleanse the camps of all “foreign elements” (i.e., non-Arabs).[12] The Army and fedayeen are working out a detailed agreement on the meaning of “heavy weapons,” which will be based on caliber, range, and whether or not the weapon is crew-served or handled by a single man. A timetable for removal is also being established, since the fedayeen argue that for logistic reasons — and to allow fear and suspicion of the Lebanese Army to die down — removal of heavy weapons cannot take place all at once or right away. In the removal of foreigners, the fedayeen made one exception: those engaged in medical work. All “combatants” will go, and this explicitly includes Turks and Iranians[13] as well as a variety of others (some of whom have been rounded up by the Lebanese Army at checkpoints outside of the camps over the past two weeks). Dib and the Foreign Minister agreed that so-called medical personnel would have to be watched carefully, and said that the fedayeen would have to be watched carefully on every point, every step of the way.

3. Control of Camps
Lebanese security forces (Army and civilian) will have checkpoints just outside the camps in strategic locations from which they can observe the interior of the camps and monitor comings and goings. There is to be no more military training in the camps, and the camps are no longer to serve as shelters for fugitives from Lebanese justice. (We understand from a separate reliable source that the Palestinian Armed Struggle Command will still have authority within the camps but will cooperate closely with Lebanese security forces with respect to fugitives from justice.) The Foreign Minister and Dib said that Lebanese security forces will have the right to enter the camps but with permission of the fedayeen.[14] The fedayeen have no right to circulate with arms outside of the camps and must use only vehicles with special plates.

4. Information/Propaganda
All information media are supposed to be consolidated under the PLO, and there are to be no more attacks on the GOL by fedayeen media, even via the Voice of Palestine in Baghdad and Damascus. Beirut is no longer to be used as a base for releasing fedayeen communiqués and announcements, although WAFA[15] (Palestine News Agency) will be allowed to continue to operate in Lebanon. Where tracts and other “wildcat” fedayeen publications are concerned, the GOL is free to act under Lebanese law as it would against any other such publication.

5. Border Areas
The fedayeen have again agreed to respect the limits drawn up by the Army following the September 16–17, 1972 Israeli action. There are to be no cross-border actions of any kind. The fedayeen are to be absent completely from the western area (vicinity of Ras Naqura) and at least 8–10 kilometers back from the border in the central area (vicinity of Bint Jbeil). In the Arqoub, the fedayeen are to remain north of the road from Hasbaya to Shebaa, except for two or three specified and carefully controlled spots.[16]

6. Comment
Obviously there are many details still to be worked out in the arrangements between the GOL and the fedayeen. The Army is being very wary and vigilant. The GOL’s public presentation of the arrangements as unilateral concessions is likely to be countered on the fedayeen side by the claim that it is all within the context of the Cairo Accords,[17] which are still in force. This is not the case — but on the other hand there is a mutual, albeit one-sided, agreement between the GOL and the fedayeen. The GOL appears to have come out very well in terms of what has been said. The big test will be in implementation, as the GOL and the Army seem to understand.

HOUGHTON[18]

SUBJECT: GOL REQUEST FOR USG ASSISTANCE
REF: STATE 94202

SUMMARY. GOL HAS OBTAINED FROM FATAH, PFLP AND PDFLP SPECIFIC CONCESSIONS
(SEPTEL) WHICH GO BEYOND MINIMAL DEMANDS REPORTED EARLIER. IT IS ON BASIS OF
FEDAYEEN ACCEPTANCE THESE SPECIFIC POINTS THAT GOL WOULD LIKE US TO MAKE
DEMARCHES DISCUSSED REFTEL. DEMARCHES WOULD BE IN SUPPORT OF FULL
IMPLEMENTATION OF PROMISES MADE BY FEDAYEEN ORGANIZATIONS, WHICH GOL INTENDS
PROVIDE ARAB AND CERTAIN OTHER GOVTS THROUGH ITS OWN DIPLOMATIC CHANNELS. USSR

POSITION REMAINS VERY UNCLEAR. CONCERNING ISRAEL, CHARGE INFORMED FONMIN AND DIB
OUR ESTIMATE OF ISRAELI POSITION RE LEBANON AND INDICATED WE HAD RECENTLY BEEN
IN TOUCH WITH ISRAELIS ON GENERAL PROBLEM. END SUMMARY.

1. CHARGE AND EMBOFF MET MORNING MAY 18 WITH FONMIN ABOU HAMAD, PRESIDENCY
DIRECTOR-GENERAL DIB AND FONOFF SEC-GEN SADAQA TO INFORM THEM SUBSTANCE
CONTENTS REFTEL. CHARGE ALSO SAID THAT SINCE LAST MEETING ON MAY 15 WE HAD
APPROACHED USSR AGAIN IN MOSCOW AND HAD BEEN IN CONTACT WITH ISRAELIS RE GENERAL
PROBLEM WHICH GOL FACING AT PRESENT. CHARGE GAVE GROUP DEPT'S ESTIMATE RE
ISRAELI INTENTIONS ALONG LINES PARA 6 REFTEL. SADAQA ASKED WHAT USG WOULD DO

IT NOT POSSIBLE TO SAY WHAT ACTION WE WOULD TAKE IN VAGUE HYPOTHETICAL
CIRCUMSTANCES SADAQA HAD MENTIONED. FONMIN APPEARED WELL SATISFIED WITH OUR
POSITION VIS-A-VIS ISRAEL.

2. AFTER INFORMING GOL OF OUR WILLINGNESS MAKE DEMARCHES REQUESTED OF US, CHARGE
ASKED FONMIN IF HE COULD NOT BE CLEARER RE SORT OF DEMARCHE GOL HAS IN MIND AND
WHEN THEY SHOULD BE MADE, PARTICULARLY IN VIEW OF REPORTS THAT GOL AND FEDAYEEN
HAD REACHED AGREEMENT IN MIXED COMMISSION EVENING OF MAY 17. FONMIN ASKED DIB TO
EXPLAIN JUST WHERE GOL STOOD WITH FEDAYEEN SINCE THIS ESSENTIAL BACKGROUND FOR
DETERMINING HOW TO PITCH DEMARCHE. DIB'S REPORT BEING SENT SEPTEL, BUT IN
SUMMARY GOL HAS OBTAINED FROM FEDAYEEN GREATER CONCESSIONS THAN THOSE LISTED AS
MINIMAL DEMANDS. FEDAYEEN CONCESSIONS ARE IN FORM OF UNILATERAL PROMISES UNDERTAKE
CERTAIN ACTIONS AND NOT RPT NOT IN FORM OF NEW GOL-FEDAYEEN AGREEMENT. ARMY IS TO
PREPARE PAPER INCORPORATING THESE PROMISES WHICH GOL WILL PROVIDE TO ARAB GOVTS
AND CERTAIN OTHER GOVTS IN ORDER THAT THERE BE NO MISUNDERSTANDING AS TO SUBSTANCE
OF FUTURE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN GOL AND FEDAYEEN. HOWEVER, NOW THAT FEDAYEEN HAVE
ACCEPTED, THE MOST IMPORTANT PROBLEM BEGINS OF BRINGING ABOUT IMPLEMENTATION OF
PROMISES AND ASSURING THAT THERE NO BACKSLIDING BY FEDAYEEN. ARMY AND FEDAYEEN
WORKING ON MODALITIES AND TIME-TABLE FOR IMPLEMENTATION AT PRESENT TIME. ANOTHER
OUTSTANDING PROBLEM IS FACT THAT SAIQA AND PFLP/GC HAVE NOT DIRECTLY AND
EXPLICITLY AGREED TO COMMITMENTS MADE BY OTHERS. FATAH, PFLP AND PDFLP REPS ON
MIXED COMMISSION STATE THEY SPEAKING FOR ALL FEDAYEEN ORGANIZATIONS, BUT GOL DOES
NOT RPT NOT ACCEPT THIS AS NECESSARILY SO. PROBLEM OF PFLP/GC IS OF LESSER
MAGNITUDE THAN THAT OF SAIQA, SINCE LATTER REFLECTS ATTITUDE OF SYRIAN GOVERNMENT
AND OF COURSE HAS MORE MEN.

3. ABOUHAMAD SAID HE THOUGHT USG DEMARCHES TO SAUDI ARABIA, KUWAIT, ABU DHABI AND
IRAN (AND ANY FURTHER TALKS WE MIGHT HAVE WITH JORDAN) SHOULD STRESS VITAL
IMPORTANCE TO LEBANON AND ENTIRE REGION OF IMPLEMENTATION OF FEDAYEEN PROMISES,
SINCE GOL FAILURE TO ESTABLISH ITS SOVEREIGNTY OVER ITS OWN TERRITORY AND THOSE
LIVING THEREIN (AS OTHER ARAB GOVTS HAVE DONE) WOULD SURELY RESULT IN ULTIMATE
DESTRUCTION OF PRO-WESTERN, DEMOCRATIC, FREE-ENTERPRISE PRINCIPLES ON WHICH
LEBANESE SYSTEM RESTS, AS WELL AS CREATE NEW SOURCE OF MAJOR TENSION IN AREA
WHICH NONE OF COUNTRIES TO BE APPROACHED WOULD WANT. GOL HAS NO RPT NO INTENTION
OF "LIQUIDATING" FEDAYEEN MOVEMENT AND WISHES PRESERVE GOOD RELATIONS WITH THEM
WITHIN LIMITATIONS DICTATED BY LEBANESE SOVEREIGNTY. GOL HAS ALREADY SPOKEN TO
ARAB GOVTS, EXPLAINING ITS CASE, AND WILL DO SO AGAIN EARLY NEXT WEEK WHILE
PASSING ALONG COPY OF FEDAYEEN PROMISES. SUBSEQUENT SUPPORTING DEMARCHE BY USG,
AND IF POSSIBLE BY OTHER GOVTS (WE ASSUME HE MEANT FRANCE AND ENGLAND AND PERHAPS
OTHER WESTERN EUROPEANS) WOULD ADD CONSIDERABLE WEIGHT TO GOL DEMARCHE. IMPORTANT
THING IS TO ENSURE THAT FEDAYEEN KEEP THEIR PROMISES IN FACT AND THAT AS TIME
GOES ON THEY NOT BE ALLOWED BACKSLIDE. GOL INTENDS SUPERVISE THIS VERY CLOSELY
BUT WILL NEED SUPPORT FROM GOVTS WHICH CONTRIBUTE MOST TO FEDAYEEN COFFERS.

4. CONCERNING SOVS, ABOU HAMAD SAID THEY CONTINUE BE MOST IMPORTANT GOVT IN TERMS
OF ABILITY INFLUENCE SITUATION FOR GOOD OR BAD. THEY HAD DIRECT INFLUENCE ON
FEDAYEEN IN LEBANON AS WELL AS ON THEIR LEFT-WING ALLIES SUCH AS LEBANESE
COMMUNIST PARTY AND KAMAL JUMBLATT. THEY ALSO HAVE MAJOR INDIRECT INFLUENCE
THROUGH THEIR STRONG POSITION IN DAMASCUS AND BAGHDAD WHICH ARE MAJOR SOURCES
OUTSIDE TROUBLE FOR LEBANON. ONE OF FRANGIE'S SPECIFIC OBJECTIVES IS TO OBTAIN
EXPLICIT COMMITMENT BY SAIQA TO PROMISES MADE BY OTHER FEDAYEEN ORGANIZATIONS AND
THIS WOULD DEPEND UPON ATTITUDE OF SARG. USSR COULD BE VERY HELPFUL ON THIS
SPECIFIC POINT AS WELL AS IN COUNSELLING MODERATION GENERALLY ON SARG AND OTHERS.

5. ABOUHAMAD AND DIB CLOSED MEETING BY THANKING US FOR ALL SUPPORT USG HAS
ALREADY PROVIDED AND FOR WHATEVER MORE WE CAN DO. THEY REPORTED THEIR CONVICTION
THAT ONLY WAY TO AVOID ANOTHER, MORE SERIOUS EXPLOSION IN LEBANON IS FOR FEDAYEEN
TO ACTUALLY MAKE GOOD ON PROMISES AND THEN TRY NOT BACK AWAY FROM THEM WITH
PASSAGE OF TIME. SUPPORT FROM VARIOUS OUTSIDE GOVTS WHOM USG WILL APPROACH WILL
BE VITAL IN THIS PROCESS.

HOUGHTON

SUBJECT: GOL-FEDAYEEN ARRANGEMENT
REF: STATE 94202

SUMMARY: FEDAYEEN REPS IN MIXED COMMISSION CAME UP WITH LIST OF SPECIFIC PROMISES
EVENING MAY 17 ON ACTIONS THEY WOULD TAKE IN ACCORDANCE WITH PRESIDENT FRANGIE'S
DEMAND THAT GOL SOVEREIGNTY HENCEFORTH BE FULLY RESPECTED. LIST COVERS COMMITMENT
NOT TO UNDERTAKE CROSS-BORDER RAIDS, TO STAY WELL BACK FROM SENSITIVE BORDER

TO REMOVE ALL "FOREIGN ELEMENTS" (I.E., NON-ARABS) AND TO ALLOW LEBANESE SECURITY

AND THEN BE RESPECTED OVER TIME TO BE WORTHWHILE, AND THAT FEDAYEEN GOOD FAITH IN
THIS REGARD IS SUSPECT. ARMY PRESENTLY WORKING OUT DETAILED AGREEMENT WHEREBY
FEDAYEEN WILL BE SUPPOSED TO IMPLEMENT THEIR PROMISES. THESE COMMITMENTS BY
FEDAYEEN APPLY TO ALL 15 REFUGEE CAMPS NOT ONLY THOSE IN BEIRUT AREA. END SUMMARY.

1. IN CONVERSATION WITH FONMIN REPORTED SEPTEL, DIRECTOR GENERAL OF PRESIDENCY
(DIB) BRIEFED CHARGE AND EMBOFF MORNING MAY 18 ON STATUS OF GOL-FEDAYEEN TALKS
WHICH CONCLUDED EVENING MAY 17. DIB AND FONMIN BOTH STRESSED ON SEVERAL OCCASIONS
THAT THERE WAS NO RPT NO AGREEMENT OR EVEN UNDERSTANDING BETWEEN GOL AND FEDAYEEN.
RATHER, LATTER HAD MADE SERIES OF COMMITMENTS OR PROMISES TO ARMY NEGOTIATORS
WHICH GOL HAS ACCEPTED AS BASIS FOR NEW RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN ITSELF AND ALL
FEDAYEEN IN LEBANON. COMMITMENTS MADE EVENING OF MAY 17 WILL BE DRAWN UP ON PIECE
OF PAPER BY ARMY AND WE CERTAIN OTHER GOVTS WILL RECEIVE COPIES. ARMY TALKING
RIGHT NOW TO FEDAYEEN REPS ABOUT MODALITIES OF IMPLEMENTATION, INCLUDING TIMETABLE.
DIB THEN SUMMED UP (FROM MEMORY) ESSENTIAL POINTS OF FEDAYEEN COMMITMENTS. (THESE
ARE REPORTED AS FOLLOWS BUT MAY NOT BE COMPLETE NOR COMPLETELY ACCURATE. WE SHALL
OBTAIN FURTHER INFO AND PRECISION WHEN AVAILABLE.)

2. ACTIVITY IN CAMPS: FEDAYEEN HAVE AGREED TO CEASE ALL TRAINING IN CAMPS, TO
REMOVE "HEAVY WEAPONS" FROM CAMPS, AND TO CLEANSE CAMPS OF ALL "FOREIGN ELEMENTS"
(I.E., NON-ARABS). ARMY AND FEDAYEEN WORKING OUT DETAILED AGREEMENT ON MEANING OF
HEAVY WEAPONS WHICH WILL BE BASED ON CALIBER, RANGE AND WHETHER OR NOT WEAPON IS
CREW-SERVED OR HANDLED BY SINGLE MAN. TIME-TABLE FOR REMOVAL ALSO BEING ESTABLISHED
SINCE FEDAYEEN ARGUE THAT FOR LOGISTIC REASONS AND TO ALLOW FEAR AND SUSPICION OF
LEBANESE ARMY TO DIE DOWN, REMOVAL OF HEAVY WEAPONS CANNOT TAKE PLACE ALL AT ONCE
AND RIGHT AWAY. IN REMOVAL OF FOREIGNERS, FEDAYEEN MADE ONE EXCEPTION AND THAT IS
THOSE WHO ENGAGED IN MEDICAL WORK. ALL "COMBATTANTS" WILL GO AND THIS EXPLICITLY
INCLUDES TURKS AND IRANIANS AS WELL AS VARIETY OF OTHERS (SOME OF WHOM HAVE BEEN
ROUNDED UP BY LEBANESE ARMY AT CHECKPOINTS OUTSIDE OF CAMPS IN PAST TWO WEEKS).
DIB AND FONMIN AGREED THAT SO-CALLED MEDICAL PERSONNEL WOULD HAVE TO BE WATCHED
CAREFULLY AND SAID THAT FEDAYEEN WOULD HAVE TO BE WATCHED CAREFULLY ON EVERY POINT,
EVERY STEP OF THE WAY.

3. CONTROL OF CAMPS: LEBANESE SECURITY FORCES (ARMY AND CIVILIAN) WILL HAVE
CHECKPOINTS JUST OUTSIDE CAMPS IN STRATEGIC LOCATIONS FROM WHICH THEY CAN OBSERVE
INTERIOR OF CAMPS ON COMINGS AND GOINGS. THERE IS TO BE NO MORE MILITARY TRAINING
IN CAMPS AND CAMPS ARE NO LONGER TO SERVE AS SHELTERS FOR FUGITIVES FROM LEBANESE
JUSTICE. (WE UNDERSTAND FROM SEPARATE RELIABLE SOURCE THAT PALESTINIAN ARMED
STRUGGLE COMMAND WILL STILL HAVE AUTHORITY WITHIN CAMPS BUT WILL COOPERATE CLOSELY
WITH LEBANESE SECURITY FORCES WITH RESPECT TO FUGITIVES FROM JUSTICE.) FONMIN AND
DIB SAID THAT LEBANESE SECURITY FORCES WILL HAVE RIGHT TO ENTER CAMPS BUT WITH
PERMISSION OF FEDAYEEN. FEDAYEEN HAVE NO RIGHT TO CIRCULATE WITH ARMS OUTSIDE OF
CAMPS AND MUST USE ONLY VEHICLES WITH SPECIAL PLATES.

4. INFORMATION/PROPAGANDA: ALL INFO MEDIA SUPPOSED TO BE CONSOLIDATED UNDER PLO
AND THERE IS TO BE NO MORE ATTACKS ON GOL BY FEDAYEEN MEDIA, EVEN VIA VOICE OF
PALESTINE IN BAGHDAD AND DAMASCUS. BEIRUT NO LONGER TO BE USED AS BASE FOR
RELEASING FEDAYEEN COMMUNIQUES AND ANNOUNCEMENTS ALTHOUGH WAFA (PALESTINE NEWS
AGENCY) WILL BE ALLOWED TO CONTINUE TO OPERATE IN LEBANON. WHERE TRACTS AND OTHER
"WILDCAT" FEDAYEEN PUBLICATIONS CONCERNED, GOL FREE TO ACT UNDER LEBANESE LAW AS
IT WOULD AGAINST ANY OTHER SUCH PUBLICATION.

5. BORDER AREAS: FEDAYEEN HAVE AGAIN AGREED TO RESPECT LIMITS DRAWN UP BY ARMY
FOLLOWING SEPT 16-17, 1972 ISRAELI ACTION. THERE ARE TO BE NO RPT NO CROSS-BORDER
ACTIONS OF ANY KIND, FEDAYEEN TO BE ABSENT COMPLETELY FROM WESTERN AREA (VICINITY
RAS NAQURAH) AND AT LEAST 8-10 KMS BACK FROM BORDER IN CENTRAL AREA (VICINITY
BINT JBEIL). IN ARKUB, FEDAYEEN TO BE NORTH OF ROAD FROM HASBAYAH TO CHEBAA
EXCEPT FOR TWO OR THREE SPECIFIED AND CAREFULLY CONTROLLED SPOTS.

6. COMMENT: OBVIOUSLY THERE ARE MANY DETAILS STILL TO BE WORKED OUT IN ARRANGEMENTS
BETWEEN GOL AND FEDAYEEN. ARMY IS BEING VERY WARY AND VIGILANT. PUBLIC PRESENTATION
OF ARRANGEMENTS BY GOL AS UNILATERAL CONCESSIONS IS LIKELY BE COUNTERED ON FEDAYEEN
SIDE BY CLAIM THAT IT IS ALL WITHIN CONTEXT CAIRO ACCORDS WHICH STILL IN FORCE.
THIS IS NOT CASE BUT ON OTHER HAND THERE IS A MUTUAL -- ALBEIT ONE-SIDED --
AGREEMENT BETWEEN GOL AND FEDAYEEN. GOL APPEARS TO HAVE COME OUT VERY WELL IN
TERMS OF WHAT HAS BEEN SAID. BIG TEST WILL BE IN IMPLEMENTATION, AS GOL AND ARMY
SEEM UNDERSTAND.

HOUGHTON
footnotes: SEPTEL (Separate Telegram): Standard State Department cable shorthand directing the reader to a companion cable filed under a different subject heading and cable number. The two cables in this merged entry are explicitly cross-referenced as SEPTELs: 1973BEIRUT05755 mentions "DIB'S REPORT BEING SENT SEPTEL," referring to 05776; while 05776 opens with "IN CONVERSATION WITH FONMIN REPORTED SEPTEL," referring back to 05755. Filed 90 minutes apart on May 18, 1973, neither is fully intelligible without the other — which is why they are archived here as a merged entry.

Démarche (French: “step” or “move”): A formal diplomatic approach in which one government makes a direct, official representation to another. A démarche is more weighty than an informal contact but does not necessarily carry the force of an ultimatum. What the GOL was requesting here was a coordinated diplomatic campaign by the United States to press Arab Gulf governments, Iran, Jordan, and — above all — the Soviet Union to use their financial and political influence to ensure the fedayeen kept the commitments they had just made. The GOL was, in effect, asking Washington to function as a guarantor of an arrangement the Lebanese themselves doubted would hold.

Saʿiqa (الصاعقة, “Thunderbolt”): Palestinian armed faction founded in 1966 under the direct sponsorship of the Syrian Ba’ath Party. Unlike Fatah, the PFLP, or the PDFLP, Saʿiqa was not an independent Palestinian movement: it was effectively an instrument of Syrian state policy. This is why the GOL’s inability to obtain Saʿiqa’s explicit acceptance of the Melkart commitments was so significant: it meant that Syria’s proxy force — and by extension, Syria — was not bound by any of the arrangements being negotiated. The cable makes this explicit: Frangieh’s specific objective was to get Saʿiqa to sign on, and this “would depend upon the attitude of the SARG.” Syria’s non-commitment was not a gap that could be negotiated around.

Chargé d’Affaires (or simply “Chargé”): The acting head of a diplomatic mission when the Ambassador is absent. The use of “Chargé” rather than “Ambassador” here indicates that Dwight Houghton was not present for the May 18 meeting, with his deputy acting in his stead. Houghton’s name still appears on the cable as the responsible officer. This is standard practice: cables are signed by the Ambassador regardless of who conducts the actual meeting.

Foreign Minister Abou Hamad: The cable uses “Abou Hamad” as the standard rendering of the Lebanese Foreign Minister’s name. Some diplomatic records from this period suggest this is a reference to Fouad Butros (Fuad Butros), who served as Foreign Minister in the cabinet of Prime Minister Takieddine Solh from July 1973. If this meeting took place on May 18, 1973, the incumbent Foreign Minister may have been someone else in the transitional period after the May 1973 crisis — or “Abou Hamad” may be a rendering of a different minister. The cable is consistent in using “Abou Hamad” throughout, suggesting this is a kunya (Arabic patronymic form of address) for a specific individual whose given name is not provided. This uncertainty is noted; the archival identification is provisional.

Presidency Director-General Dib: The recurring GOL interlocutor throughout the May 1973 crisis cables. The Presidency Director-General was the senior official of the Lebanese Presidential Palace, functioning as the head of the presidential administration and a key channel between President Frangieh and foreign diplomats. “Dib” appears in several cables as the GOL’s senior briefing officer on the fedayeen negotiations. His role here — summing up from memory the full terms of the fedayeen commitments — indicates he was at the center of the negotiation.

Mixed Commission: The joint body of Lebanese Army officers and fedayeen representatives established to manage the practical implementation of agreements governing Palestinian armed presence in Lebanon. The Mixed Commission operated under the framework of the 1969 Cairo Agreement, which had created a formal structure for GOL-PLO relations. By May 1973, the Mixed Commission had been the venue for ten days of intensive negotiations following the outbreak of fighting on May 7–8. The evening of May 17 — when the fedayeen made their commitments — was the concluding session of this round of talks.

This is the central legal and political framing of the entire Melkart arrangement, and it was chosen deliberately by the Lebanese government. By insisting the fedayeen commitments were “unilateral promises” rather than “a new GOL-fedayeen agreement,” the Lebanese were attempting to sidestep the Cairo Accords framework. Any new “agreement” would implicitly have operated within that framework — which the fedayeen would use to argue their presence and operations were legitimized under the 1969 accords. Unilateral promises, by contrast, were not framed as bilateral contractual obligations with reciprocal GOL concessions; they were simply undertakings the fedayeen made. This distinction mattered enormously on paper. In practice, the fedayeen would interpret the arrangements as a supplement to the Cairo Accords — exactly as the Embassy predicted in paragraph 6 of 05776.

Kamal Jumblatt (1917–1977): Leader of the Progressive Socialist Party and paramount chief of the Lebanese Druze community. In 1973, Jumblatt was the leading figure of the Lebanese left-wing political coalition that aligned itself with the Palestinian fedayeen and maintained close ties to Syria and the Soviet Union. The Foreign Minister’s identification of Jumblatt as a Soviet “left-wing ally” and thus an indirect channel of Soviet influence on Lebanon documents the GOL’s 1973 threat assessment. Jumblatt would go on to lead the Lebanese National Movement (LNM) — the leftist-Palestinian alliance — during the 1975–76 civil war. He was assassinated in March 1977, almost certainly by Syrian agents, after President Assad turned against him.

This sentence is the Foreign Minister’s own prediction, delivered at the moment of apparent diplomatic success, that the agreement would fail and a worse explosion would follow. The phrase “another, more serious explosion” acknowledges that the May 7–8 fighting was the first such explosion. The GOL is predicting the next one while still sitting in the meeting that resolved the current one. The historical record shows the prediction was correct: the fedayeen did not fully implement the Melkart commitments, the Lebanese Army’s capacity to enforce them degraded, and the “more serious explosion” came in April 1975. Abou Hamad’s words were in the diplomatic record in May 1973.

The GOL’s own summary document for the arrangement that would become known as the Melkart Protocol contains an explicit statement of doubt about the other party’s good faith. This is not an external skeptical assessment — it is the Lebanese government’s own framing, transmitted through U.S. Embassy reporting, on the day after the commitments were made. The Melkart Protocol has sometimes been described in secondary literature as a genuine attempt to regulate Palestinian armed presence. The cable record suggests the GOL itself regarded it as an instrument whose value depended entirely on enforcement — and already doubted the good faith of the party making the promises.

“Foreign elements” (non-Arabs) in the camps: This term is used as a euphemism for international volunteers and fighters who had joined the Palestinian armed organizations — individuals from outside the Arab world who had come to Lebanon to participate in the fedayeen cause. The cable makes clear that the category includes “Turks and Iranians as well as a variety of others,” some of whom had already been rounded up by the Lebanese Army at checkpoints in the preceding two weeks. This documents, from a 1973 U.S. Embassy source, that Palestinian camps in Lebanon housed non-Arab combatants including Turks and Iranians. The international composition of the fedayeen forces was therefore documented in the diplomatic record 50 years before it became a matter of historical dispute.

The explicit naming of “Turks and Iranians” as “combatants” in the Palestinian refugee camps is among the most historically specific details in these cables. Pre-revolutionary Iran (1973) under the Shah was not generally associated with Palestinian armed factions. The Iranian government was a U.S. ally and the Shah had diplomatic relations with Israel. Yet the Embassy’s reporting — drawn from Dib’s direct briefing — names Iranians among the non-Arab combatants whom the fedayeen themselves committed to remove from the camps. This detail is in the U.S. diplomatic record as of May 18, 1973. It has not appeared in standard accounts of the Palestinian armed presence in Lebanon.

The phrase “with permission of the fedayeen” qualifies the entire clause about Lebanese sovereignty over the camps. Formally, Lebanese security forces were being granted the right of access. Practically, they would need to ask the fedayeen for permission to exercise that right. The GOL and Dib were apparently satisfied with this formulation — or at least accepted it as the best that could be obtained. The Embassy’s Comment paragraph (para. 6) implicitly registers skepticism: “the big test will be in implementation.” A right of entry that requires the consent of the party being entered is, in practice, not a right of entry.

WAFA (وكالة أنباء فلسطين, Wikalat Anbaʼ Falastin — Palestine News Agency): The official PLO news wire service, founded in 1972. The Melkart commitments required the fedayeen to cease using Beirut as a base for propaganda releases. WAFA was explicitly carved out of this prohibition — it was allowed to continue operating in Lebanon. This carve-out for the PLO’s official news agency, while nominally modest, preserved a key institutional presence in Beirut. WAFA still operates today as the official Palestinian news agency.

The geographical specifics here document the military geography of the Melkart Protocol in a level of detail not generally available in secondary sources. Ras Naqura (also known as Rosh HaNikra) is the Mediterranean coastal point on the Lebanese-Israeli border; total fedayeen exclusion there. Bint Jbeil, in the central south, required an 8–10 km pullback. The Arqoub (العرقوب) — the southeastern corner of Lebanon where the Lebanese, Syrian, and Israeli borders converge, historically the most active base for cross-border fedayeen operations — was subject to the most permissive terms: fedayeen to remain north of the Hasbaya-Shebaa road except for “two or three specified and carefully controlled spots.” The Arqoub had been known informally as “Fatahland” since the late 1960s. The gap between the formal commitment (north of Hasbaya-Shebaa road) and the exceptions (“two or three spots” to be specified) left substantial room for contested interpretation.

Cairo Agreement (November 3, 1969): The foundational document governing PLO–GOL relations, signed by PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat and Lebanese Army Commander General Emile Bustani under Egyptian mediation. The Agreement formally legalized the PLO’s armed presence on Lebanese soil and granted Palestinian organizations authority within the refugee camps. The GOL insisted the Melkart commitments were “unilateral promises” rather than a new agreement specifically to avoid the implication that they operated under the Cairo Accords framework. The Embassy predicted in para. 6 that the fedayeen would nonetheless frame the Melkart arrangement as “within the context of the Cairo Accords” — which is exactly what happened.

Dwight J. Houghton: U.S. Ambassador to Lebanon 1970–1974. These two cables, filed on May 18, 1973, represent Houghton’s reporting on the moment of apparent resolution of the May 1973 crisis — the fedayeen commitments that would be formalized as the Melkart Protocol. Read together with the earlier cables in this archive (1973BEIRUT04974 documenting the April 30 bomb plot; 1973BEIRUT05155 and 1973BEIRUT05159 documenting the May 7–8 fighting; and 1973BEIRUT05437 assessing the likely terms), the Melkart cables are the conclusion of a crisis that was, in the Embassy’s own terms at the time, unlikely to resolve the underlying structural problem. Houghton left Beirut in 1974. He did not see the war that his cables had predicted.

readerNarrative.summary: On May 18, 1973, U.S. Embassy Beirut filed two classified cables 90 minutes apart documenting the conclusion of the negotiations that produced the Melkart Protocol. The first cable (1973BEIRUT05755) records the Lebanese Foreign Minister and Presidency Director-General briefing the U.S. Chargé on what had been achieved and what American diplomatic support was being requested. The second (1973BEIRUT05776) documents the specific commitments: a pullback from border areas, removal of heavy weapons from camps, no cross-border raids, Lebanese security force access to camps, and removal of non-Arab “foreign elements” — explicitly including Turks and Iranians. Both cables are marked SECRET/EXDIS. Together they confirm: the Lebanese government called these “unilateral promises,” not an agreement; Saʿiqa explicitly did not sign; the GOL’s own diplomats described fedayeen good faith as “suspect”; and Lebanese forces could enter camps only with fedayeen permission.

The Embassy predicted the fedayeen would nonetheless claim the arrangement was “within the context” of those same Accords.

Saʿiqa — Syria’s proxy faction — explicitly did not sign the Melkart commitments. Fatah, PFLP, and PDFLP representatives claimed they were speaking for all fedayeen. The GOL did not accept this. Syria’s armed proxy was thus entirely outside the arrangement from the moment it was made.

The GOL’s own summary of the arrangement, transmitted through the U.S. Embassy, states that “fedayeen good faith in this regard is suspect.” This is not an outside assessment. It is the Lebanese government’s own language, on record in May 1973.

Lebanese security forces were granted the right to enter the refugee camps “with permission of the fedayeen.” Sovereignty in name, with the party to be regulated retaining veto power over the act of regulation.

Non-Arab combatants in the Palestinian camps — required to leave under the Melkart terms — explicitly included Turks and Iranians, documented by U.S. Embassy reporting based on the Presidency Director-General’s direct briefing. This is in the diplomatic record as of May 18, 1973.

His prediction was accurate. His name as given in the cables (“Abou Hamad”) appears to be a kunya; the archival identification remains provisional.

keyFigures.desc: Saʿiqa’s explicit non-acceptance of the Melkart commitments is the most consequential single fact in these two cables. As an arm of Syrian Ba’ath Party policy rather than an independent Palestinian organization, Saʿiqa’s position reflected Damascus’s decision not to be bound. The entire arrangement was therefore built on a foundation where Syria’s proxy force — the one with the most men and the deepest external backing — was formally outside it.
